title: fix(tests): collect checkpoint source pod logs before cleanup
body:
## Summary

Collect checkpoint source pod diagnostics in a dedicated `checkpoint/` artifact directory before `ManagedDeployment` deletes the deployment, without attempting metrics scrapes on those source pods.

The operator already stamps DGD-name and component labels onto SnapshotJob source pod templates, so the existing service collector already selected these pods before deletion. This change makes checkpoint diagnostics easier to locate and skips unnecessary metrics collection; it does not establish that the old collector missed source pods in [the motivating CI failure](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/actions/runs/34444478883/job/102771685192?pr=14105).

## Details

- Discover SnapshotJobs using the DGD label, then select source pods using the SnapshotJob name and UID. The UID prevents matching pods belonging to an older job with a reused name.
- Save manifests and per-container current and available previous logs under `<log_dir>/checkpoint/` before ordinary service collection and deployment deletion.
- Exclude a source pod from subsequent service collection only after its manifest and all current container logs have been saved. If collection fails, leave it eligible for the existing service collector, including its metrics attempt. Missing previous-instance logs do not trigger fallback.
- Treat missing SnapshotJob CRDs and API collection failures as best-effort diagnostics so cleanup can continue.

Collection requires the pod to still exist when cleanup starts. It cannot recover artifacts from already deleted pods or fix the underlying checkpoint failure. The later workflow cluster dump can still omit deleted pods; manifests collected here are separate files such as `checkpoint/<pod-name>.yaml`.

## Validation

- Reproduced suppressed fallback through `ManagedDeployment.__aexit__` with mocked Kubernetes APIs and real artifact writes: transient manifest-fetch, current-log-fetch, and file-write failures each failed before the fix and passed afterward.
- All 27 targeted helper tests passed on Python 3.12 with isolated pytest configuration (`--noconftest -o addopts='' -o filterwarnings=''`). Coverage checks artifacts before deletion, original test-failure propagation, successful-collection deduplication, optional previous logs, and API failures.
- Pre-commit checks for both changed files and `git diff --check` passed.
- Live-cluster checkpoint E2E was not run locally because no Kubernetes context is configured.

title: feat(completions): forward backend multimodal data
body:
## Summary

Adds a documented channel for custom-modality inputs on the Completions API, for models that register their own vLLM multimodal processor.

Today a completion request has no field that can carry them, and no existing field can be repurposed:

- **An unrecognized top-level field never reaches the worker.** By default it is rejected at admission — `Unsupported parameter(s): \`multi_modal_data\`` — unless it is one of the six named `PASSTHROUGH_EXTRA_FIELDS`. With `DYN_IGNORE_OPENAI_FE_UNSUPPORTED_FIELDS` set it is dropped instead of rejected. Either way the payload is gone before preprocessing.
- **`multi_modal_data` on the internal wire is frontend-owned.** `MultimodalDataMap`'s variants (`Url | RawUrl | Decoded(RdmaMediaDataDescriptor)`) are produced by the preprocessor from chat content parts; it is not a client-writable request field on either endpoint.
- **`prompt_embeds` replaces the entire prompt**, so it cannot express "text plus one custom modality" — the client would have to own the LM embedding table.
- **`mm_processor_kwargs` is chat-only.** `NvCreateCompletionRequest` does not implement `OAIChatLikeRequest::mm_processor_kwargs`, so it resolves to the trait default `None` and the completions operator never reads it. Even on chat it would be insufficient alone: vLLM runs the multimodal processor only when `multi_modal_data` is non-empty.

### What changes

- **`NvCreateCompletionRequest.multi_modal_data`** — a typed, JSON-safe `map<string, any>` the frontend admits but never interprets. The key matches the engine-side name the payload is installed under.
- **`PreprocessedRequest.backend_multi_modal_data`** — the frontend-to-worker wire field. Deliberately *not* `multi_modal_data`: keeping them separate is what lets the worker tell "media the frontend already resolved" from "a payload only the engine's processor understands".
- **vLLM worker** installs the payload as the engine's `multi_modal_data`; the registered modality processor owns all value validation.

```bash
curl http://localhost:8000/v1/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "model": "<model>",
    "prompt": [1, 2, 3],
    "max_tokens": 16,
    "multi_modal_data": {
      "custom_input": {"dtype": "float32-le", "shape": [2, 4], "data_base64": "AAAAAA=="}
    }
  }'
```

### Fail-closed behavior

A silently ignored payload returns a plausible text-only answer, which is the worst outcome available. Every path that cannot install it rejects the request instead:

| Path | Behavior |
|---|---|
| vLLM, aggregated | Installs the payload |
| vLLM, disaggregated — generic models | Prefill installs it; decode continues from `expanded_prompt_token_ids` |
| vLLM, disaggregated — geometry-handoff families | Rejected |
| vLLM, text-in-text-out (`--use-vllm-tokenizer`) | Rejected |
| SGLang, TensorRT-LLM | Rejected |

Disaggregation works for models whose decode leg continues from the prefill worker's expanded prompt token IDs — the same generic handoff every model without a family-specific decode contract already uses. Families that rebuild position IDs from modality geometry (Qwen-VL rebuilds mRoPE from `image_grid_thw`) refuse the payload: Dynamo cannot derive that handoff from something it does not interpret, and generating against wrong positions is worse than failing.

The backend rejections reuse the existing `reject_unsupported_multimodal_uuids` capability-guard pattern, at the same six call sites.

### Frontend validation

The frontend enforces only the two invariants a backend cannot recover from, and leaves the values alone:

- **Empty map rejected** — it carries no payload and would otherwise trip the worker's multimodal opt-in check.
- **`prompt_embeds` combination rejected** — that replaces the whole prompt, leaving no placeholder sequence for a processor to expand.

## Validation

**Rust**

- `cargo test -p dynamo-llm --lib protocols::openai` — 502 passed
- `cargo test -p dynamo-llm --lib preprocessor` — 220 passed
- `cargo check -p dynamo-llm --all-targets` clean; `cargo fmt --all` applied

New cases in `completions.rs`: the payload is admitted without interpretation; an empty map is rejected; the `prompt_embeds` combination is rejected.

**Python**

- `components/src/dynamo/sglang/tests/` — 770 passed, 1 skipped
- `components/src/dynamo/trtllm/tests/` — 517 passed
- `components/src/dynamo/common/tests/multimodal/test_cache_uuid.py` — 14 passed
- `components/src/dynamo/vllm/tests/multimodal_utils/test_vllm_request_processor.py` — 14 cases covering this change passed

Both backend suites are green with the new capability guard in place, so the rejection path does not disturb any existing request flow.

Those cases cover: aggregated install; prefill install; decode continuing from expanded token IDs; missing-handoff rejection; Qwen-VL rejection on both P/D legs and acceptance when aggregated; rejection of an empty payload and a frontend media mix; and passthrough of frontend-named modalities (`image`, `vision_chunk`, `video_url`) on both the aggregated and prefill paths. `test_cache_uuid.py` covers the shared backend capability guard.

**End to end** — `tests/frontend/test_backend_multimodal_data.py` — 2 passed

A new `pre_merge`, `gpu_0` test that runs a real frontend against a stub worker and checks the transport claim directly, with no GPU and no engine. The worker compares the `backend_multi_modal_data` it received against an exact expected payload — nested objects, floats, booleans, an explicit null, arrays, and a base64 blob standing in for a serialized tensor — and answers 422 carrying what it actually saw on any drift, so a regression names the drift rather than just failing. Admission-time rejections are pinned by the Rust validation tests instead, so the subprocess stack is spent only on the transport boundary that needs it. The two cases are:

| Case | Asserts |
|---|---|
| `..._reaches_the_worker_unchanged` | The payload arrives as the same semantic JSON value, and does not leak into the frontend-owned media map |
| `..._omitted_payload_stays_absent` | An omitted field arrives absent, not as an empty map |

## Notes for reviewers

- The wire name differs from the request name on purpose (see above). If reviewers prefer one name end to end, `backend_multi_modal_data` on the request is a mechanical change.
- **KV routing scores this request on its placeholder prompt tokens alone**, because the frontend cannot hash a payload it does not interpret. Two requests with the same prompt and different payloads look identical to the router. vLLM folds multimodal identity into its own block hashes, so engine-side prefix caching stays correct; only the router's prefix-overlap estimate is optimistic. Documented in the vLLM reference guide.
- **Modality names are the engine processor's to choose**, including names the frontend uses for its own media. A backend-owned payload is built through a path that skips frontend UUID inference and structural pad expansion (`backend_owned` on `build_tokens_prompt`), so `compute_mm_uuids` and the Kimi pad expansion never read it. Reserving names would have banned a legitimate processor that registers a modality called `image`.

title: fix(runtime): release multimodal cache indexers after consumer teardown
body:
Shared multimodal embedding-cache indexers could remain alive after their last consumer disappeared because subscriber and endpoint-cleanup tasks retained them. Both tasks now hold weak index references and observe index-lifecycle cancellation, including during reconnect waits and subscription setup.

Cleanup watcher registrations also retain weak generation references. A retiring watcher removes only its own generation, so it cannot erase a replacement watcher registered for the same endpoint.

GitHub Rust CI passed the last-consumer cancellation, shared-registry eviction, cleanup-watcher shutdown, and replacement-generation tests on commit `a2fbd28b7b84`. The Pre Merge and full PR workflows passed on that commit, including both planner CPU architectures after retrying an image-build timeout. Closes #13335.

title: fix(discovery): release idle endpoint runtime and HiCache state
body:
ModelManager retained endpoint runtime configuration and HiCache state after consumers stopped using them. Idle endpoint cleanup now removes HiCache state after its last external owner is dropped, then closes an unused runtime-config watcher under the same entry lock used to acquire receivers. Discovery tasks also stop when their receivers close, without waiting for another discovery event.

Consumers can outlive the manager that created them, including the standalone Python router's temporary ModelManager. Dropping the manager therefore leaves their configuration watches active; explicit lifecycle cancellation occurs only when eviction establishes that a watcher has no external consumer. Prefill bindings retain their runtime-config receiver for as long as they use endpoint metadata.

Regressions cover shared ownership, endpoint cleanup, and a real discovery watch receiving configuration after its manager is dropped, followed by task exit when the final consumer drops. After merging main and resolving the worker-target import conflict, Pre Merge and full PR CI passed on `7ffe18b61a36`. The Rust lifecycle regressions and both remote-indexer routing variants passed on the updated branch. The arm64 suite passed all 3,527 selected tests in a fresh CI attempt, including the previously failing NATS-free ZMQ and AIC routing cases; the earlier timeout cause remains undetermined. Closes #13334.

title: refactor(router): centralize policy configuration and flag deprecations
body:
## Summary

Depends on #14785. This PR targets its branch while that parent is open, so the diff contains only the configuration and deprecation changes. Retarget to `main` after the parent merges.

Move routing configuration into `--router-policy-config`:

- Default-policy scoring knobs use `worker_selection.instances[].parameters`. The builtin owns the shared-cache multiplier default: `0.5` when shared cache is enabled. Policy parameters override explicit deprecated CLI/env values, including zero. This also fixes native startup giving YAML-enabled HiCache zero credit while env-enabled HiCache got `0.5`.
- Shared cache and tracking settings use a new process-wide `router` section. Python validation and Rust startup apply these settings before constructing policies and trackers. Explicit YAML values override legacy flags; omitted values keep their existing settings.
- Deprecate the six scoring flags, `--load-aware`, and the redundant prefill/decode selection and queue threshold/policy flags, including their environment variables. Their existing behavior and precedence remain available during migration.

All Python flag deprecations use one reusable `Deprecated(replacement, remove_in)` declaration through the argument helpers. It supplies the same warning format for CLI/env use and help text, including aliases and boolean negative forms. Defaults do not warn. Native Rust env reads use one matching deprecation mapping. Removal comments target v1.7, after the v1.6 YAML migration release; wire compatibility fields keep their separate lifetime.

The overlap-query response reports raw cache hits and removes `router_credit_blocks`, which was calculated from global weights and could disagree with the active policy.

Shared infrastructure flags remain supported, including host/disk cache weights because they also affect load accounting. Conditional-disaggregation settings remain separate. The migration guide replaces the load-aware preset with policy parameters and a `router` section in one YAML file.

Related: ai-dynamo/dynamo#14778.

## Validation

- 1,325 Rust tests passed; 2 ignored, across `dynamo-kv-router` and the builtin policy crate. Covers shared settings, cached startup loading, null resets, validation, policy parameters, existing selection behavior, and shared-cache defaults/explicit-zero precedence through actual worker selection.

title: refactor(router): move default worker selection into builtin plugin
body:
## Summary

Move the default worker-selection policy into `dynamo-custom-policy-builtin`, alongside the two-tier policy. The default now uses the same public filter, score, and pick API as custom policies. Routing hosts install it automatically; plugin authors do not need to register or depend on the builtin crate themselves.

Refs #14778.

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    H[Host: snapshot and eligible workers] --> F[Filters]
    F --> S[Score: costs for all candidates]
    S --> P[Pick: choose one candidate]
    P --> B[Host: validate and book capacity]
```

- **Score** receives the request context and all remaining candidates, then writes one cost per candidate. The default computes cache credit, load cost, decay, and preferred-taint cost here. Request-wide calculations happen once inside the scorer; there is no public `prepare` callback.
- **Pick** receives candidates with their summed costs and returns a row. The default handles minimum cost, ties, and temperature sampling. Unseeded sampling reads candidates directly; deterministic replay retains its sorted buffer.
- **The host** still owns eligibility, cache/load snapshots, accounting, reservations, cancellation, and completion. Peer updates reach the sequence tracker asynchronously. Plugins read the current snapshot; they do not synchronize trackers or wait for peers.

## API and configuration

- Each component declares `WorkerInputs` for the data it needs. Cache, load, and preferred-taint access is gated independently for that component. Combined CACHE requirements determine whether the host starts cache indexing. The builtin omits CACHE at zero overlap credit and for plain disaggregated decode, preserving load-only accounting.
- Cache inputs contain worker overlap estimates, tier information, and borrowed shared-cache hits. There is no separate `context.cache()`. Exact prompt length remains available through `context.prompt_tokens()`.
- Existing top-level router settings still configure the default. Named policy instances can configure `dynamo-default-cost-fn` through plugin parameters. Per-request overrides no longer replace its scoring weights or temperature.
- All in-tree plugins, examples, and affected documentation use the updated API. No compatibility shim is added.

## Validation

- **416 targeted tests passed**, covering load-only accounting, cache input gating, conditional decode, booking/release, and seeded/unseeded parity.
- All-target Clippy with warnings denied, formatting, and changed-file pre-commit passed.
- Fixed the Python test-link failure by returning a Rust error from input validation and constructing `ValueError` at the Python boundary. Both plain `cargo test --locked --no-run` and `cargo test --locked` pass without extra linker flags.

## Performance

Selection reuses candidate and cost buffers, computes request-wide values once per batch, and skips unused shared-cache scans. Warmed selection checks recorded zero allocations.

The short sampling comparison was inconclusive: 0.3% faster to 3.1% slower on a noisy shared host. The accepted stacked-scorer overhead remains a follow-up. End-to-end serving impact has not been measured.

title: fix(vllm): initialize prompt logprobs before prefix cache policy
body:
## Summary

When a token request asks for `prompt_logprobs`, Dynamo currently assigns it after constructing vLLM `SamplingParams`. The constructor has already derived `skip_reading_prefix_cache=False`, so a repeated prompt incorrectly reuses cached tokens that have no prompt logits.

Pass the requested `prompt_logprobs` into the constructor so vLLM sets its derived cache policy. Preserve model defaults, RL token-in behavior, and explicit cache-policy overrides.

## Validation

- CPU reproduction with the actual vLLM `KVCacheManager`: after warming a 39-token prompt, the original Dynamo parameters reuse 32 tokens for `prompt_logprobs=0`; native vLLM and the fix reuse zero.
- Final regression cases on the original function: 2 failed, 3 passed. Covers omitted/zero prompt logprobs, ordinary/RL requests, and explicit cache policy. Nonempty model defaults distinguish ordinary temperature inheritance from RL defaults.
- `python -m pytest components/src/dynamo/vllm/tests/test_vllm_tito_parity.py components/src/dynamo/vllm/tests/test_vllm_unit.py -q`: 191 passed.

- Original code: repeated requests with `prompt_logprobs=0` and `5` still report 256 cached tokens and omit `nvext.prompt_logprobs`, despite HTTP 200 and normal generated completions.
- Fixed code: the same requests report zero cached tokens and return all 265 prompt-logprob positions (first entry null; every remaining position contains the actual prompt token and finite probabilities). Width 0 returns one entry; width 5 returns 5–6 entries including the actual token. Ordinary repeated requests still hit 256 cached tokens. All four real HTTP cases pass.

title: fix(frontend): release vLLM streams after local stop
body:
## Summary

The token-only vLLM worker leaves string-stop detection to the Python frontend. When vLLM's `OutputProcessor` matches a stop string, Dynamo ignores `reqs_to_abort` and keeps reading the backend stream even though that choice is already finished. The eventual backend usage can then be dropped with its empty choices.

After a local stop, yield the terminal response and release the routed stream once all choices belonging to this request have finished. Derive completion usage from tokens consumed by active choices, including when the worker supplies cumulative usage. Retain the latest backend usage per request, including prompt-token and cache details from a sibling that finishes before the final local stop, and recompute total tokens. Exclude late chunks for already stopped choices from frontend usage and token metrics. The parent HTTP context and unrelated requests in the shared output processor remain active.

## Validation

Current follow-up (2026-09-22):

- Reproduced the natural-finish-before-local-stop ordering with the real vLLM 0.28.0 output processor: the previous head drops `prompt_tokens_details`. The regression now preserves `cached_tokens=64`, backend `prompt_tokens=128`, and corrected terminal totals.
- `python -m pytest components/src/dynamo/frontend/tests/test_vllm_processor_unit.py -q`: 170 passed with current-worktree Python sources and rebuilt native bindings.
- `python -m pytest tests/frontend/test_vllm_prepost_integration.py -k local_stop_preserves_stream_terminal --models-dir=/root/.cache/huggingface --durations=0 -q`: passed using real etcd/TCP/ZMQ/HTTP and the existing token worker. Setup, call, and teardown take approximately 25 seconds; the test now has a 90-second pytest timeout (3x, rounded up). This is a transport/frontend integration check, not a new GPU model-serving run.
- Applicable changed-file `pre-commit` hooks pass.

Earlier validation (historical revisions):

- Synced upstream `main` (`a5b48b0821`) on 2026-09-06 through a GitHub-verified, DCO-signed merge commit. This includes the operator documentation link fix in #14353; the three frontend file contents are unchanged by the sync. After syncing, all 163 frontend unit tests and applicable changed-file pre-commit hooks pass. The local documentation checker reports zero broken links (four pre-existing suspicious-symlink warnings only), and generated release documentation checks pass. The new remote `lychee`, Markdown link check, and DCO checks pass; other lightweight CI checks are still running. GPU and HTTP integration tests were not rerun for this base sync.
- Original code: all three new CPU cases fail; covers a stop split across token chunks, `n=2` with one choice stopping early, and another active request sharing the output processor.
- Original HTTP regression: status 200 and stop finish reason, but terminal usage is absent.
- `python -m pytest tests/frontend/test_vllm_prepost_integration.py -k local_stop_preserves_stream_terminal -q` (local model cache): 1 passed. Real etcd/TCP/HTTP with the existing token worker; two consecutive requests preserve the stop finish reason, 21 consumed output tokens in usage, and `[DONE]`.
- `pre-commit run --files` for all three changed files: passed.
- Review regressions: two late tokens for a stopped `n=2` choice inflated usage to 7 instead of 5. Coverage now checks both missing usage and worker-provided cumulative usage when the sibling naturally finishes. The worker-usage case fails against `48e2d114d4` and passes with this follow-up; prompt/cache details are retained.
- Pre-sync revision: `python -m pytest components/src/dynamo/frontend/tests/test_vllm_processor_unit.py -q` reports 163 passed. The local HTTP/etcd/TCP/ZMQ integration test and applicable pre-commit hooks also passed. The GPU results below are from the prior revision; GPU model serving was not rerun for this usage-accounting follow-up.
- Real GPU comparison: Qwen3-0.6B BF16 on RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, vLLM 0.28.0, TP=1, eager/Triton attention, Python vLLM frontend, real etcd/TCP/ZMQ. Four streamed scenarios (reference, early string stop, follow-up request, and `n=2`) preserve identical visible output across versions.
- Original code: early stop still generates all 384 backend tokens; `n=2` generates 768. Both lose terminal usage. With the fix, the single-choice request consumes/generates 18 tokens; `n=2` reports 38 consumed tokens with 39 actually generated during cancellation propagation. Both return stop finish reasons, usage, and `[DONE]`.
- For both fixed stop scenarios, worker logs contain matching `Decode Request ID` and completed `Aborted Request ID`; scheduler running/waiting gauges return to zero and the generation counter remains stable for two seconds. Follow-up requests succeed.

These are bounded correctness checks, not a cancellation-latency performance campaign. Per-choice backend cancellation for `n>1` is outside this change; the shared stream is released when all choices finish. Multi-GPU deployments were not tested.

title: feat(vllm): forward preprocessed multimodal features over tito
body:
## Overview

Forward renderer-produced preprocessed multimodal features through Dynamo's native vLLM sidecar to vLLM gRPC. This also preserves the Generate request `/inference/v1/generate` and response semantics.

### Preprocessed multimodal transport

- Decode inline `vllm_tito.features` and translate them into gRPC `PreprocessedMediaFeatures`.
- Preserve tensor payloads, multimodal placeholder ranges, and renderer metadata required by the vLLM execution path.
- Reject malformed feature envelopes, conflicting routing markers, and requests that mix raw media with preprocessed media.
- Leave the existing raw-media request path unchanged.

### Stable multimodal identity

- Derive a domain-separated identity from the decoded inline feature content.
- Use the same identity calculation in the frontend and sidecar and reject mismatches before execution.
- Scope cache identity by adapter context while retaining the content-only multimodal hash exposed to vLLM.

### Native Generate compatibility

- Advertise native Generate support now that proto 0.3 provides typed sampling, stopping, response, multimodal, and LoRA fields.
- Preserve projected sampling and stopping controls, including omitted values and explicit disabled sentinels.
- Require token IDs for the Prime-RL path and continue to reject controls that cannot be represented safely on the gRPC wire.

### Non-streaming response folding

- Preserve the terminal sampling mask when Dynamo folds token-stream responses into one non-streaming Generate response.
- Validate mask structure and token alignment instead of silently returning malformed auxiliary data.

## Scope

This PR provides multimodal feature forwarding and Generate protocol parity. Routed-expert capture and routed-expert gRPC transport are separate changes; the Nemotron validation below used those additional integration revisions together with this PR.

## Reviewer guide

1. `lib/sidecar/vllm/src/convert.rs` — feature-envelope validation, proto conversion, request semantics, and routing-marker verification.
2. `lib/llm/src/http/service/generate.rs` — request-side multimodal identity and execution-payload preservation.
3. `lib/llm/src/protocols/openai/generate.rs` — terminal sampling-mask folding for non-streaming responses.
4. `lib/sidecar/vllm/src/tests.rs` — malformed-input, compatibility, identity, and gRPC conversion coverage.

## Validation

- `cargo check -p dynamo-vllm-sidecar`
- `cargo test -p dynamo-vllm-sidecar --lib` — 68 passed
- `cargo test -p dynamo-llm generate_response_ -- --nocapture` — 16 passed with published `vllm-proto` 0.3.0
- `cargo test -p dynamo-llm --lib multimodal_routing_matches_worker_events_and_preserves_execution_payload -- --nocapture`
- `cargo test -p dynamo-llm --lib sparse_and_ambiguous_multimodal_layouts_are_handled -- --nocapture`
- `cargo test -p dynamo-llm --lib invalid_or_unsupported_multimodal_metadata_falls_back_safely -- --nocapture`
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`

### End-to-end validation

- **Qwen3.5-4B:** three image-bearing orchestrator and trainer steps, four NCCL policy receives, pre- and post-policy image probes, and clean runner exit on Dynamo `2f8beab0eac44c02a602788fb6bbc7f472db4a49` with vLLM `bf13ecc2f7c4d69b59854f7cef37547be58805e5`.

The combined integration stack advanced policies `v0` through `v3` over NCCL and synchronized both W&B runs. Rewards were `0.7500`, `0.7500`, and `0.7500`; trainer mismatch KL was `0.0062`, `0.0203`, and `0.0004`.

title: feat(examples): add remote custom encoder orchestrator
body:
_Based on #13293, #15195._

## Why

Show the application-owned topology enabled by Dynamo's maintained vLLM handoff without duplicating framework logic or introducing a workflow product. The orchestrator consumes the stable runtime-owned unary APIs, so example code does not depend on a component-only experimental namespace. Keeping its test with the example also preserves the dependency direction between reusable components and applications. Because the orchestrator registers a public chat model, it has to serve a whole conversation, not only its image turns.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Client --> Frontend

    Orchestrator --> Handoff[ExternalEncoderHandoff]

    Orchestrator -->|prepared GenerateRequest| VLLM[stock aggregated dynamo.vllm]
    VLLM -->|token stream| Unary[dynamo.llm.LLMUnaryClient]
    Unary --> Orchestrator
```

title: feat(router): add worker cache-reuse telemetry (F2-F5)
body:
## Summary

Adds always-on cache-reuse counters for each KV-routing attempt. The router records the raw cached prefix on the best eligible worker and on the selected worker/rank. The worker reports its cache-hit counts when the request completes. Routing decisions and tier weights are unchanged; reported token values are raw and uncapped.

The counters use the existing `RouterRequestMetrics` and request-guard lifecycle, with one once-only flag for completion, errors, cancellation, and dropped streams. This incorporates Neelay's reference cleanup from #15173, retaining counters rather than introducing histograms.

## Metrics and compatibility

All names below have the `dynamo_component_router_` prefix and carry `phase` (`aggregated`, `prefill`, or `decode`) and `model` labels.

| Measurement | Metric |
| --- | --- |
| Received input tokens (F0) | `input_sequence_tokens_sum` (existing histogram sum) |
| Best eligible cached prefix (F2) | `kv_best_eligible_cached_prefix_tokens_total` |
| Selected worker/rank cached prefix (F3) | `kv_selected_cached_prefix_tokens_total` |
| Worker lookup hits, when available (F4) | `kv_worker_lookup_tokens_total` |
| Backend-reported cache-hit tokens (F5) | `kv_worker_reused_tokens_total` |
| Worker reporting coverage | `kv_worker_outcomes_total{result}` |

- F0's existing histogram now excludes query-only selections and carries matching phase/model labels. Queries needing process-wide totals must sum across those labels.
- F2/F3 are recorded at selection. Worker values require successful completion and a valid prompt-matched report. The guard retains the attempt's original phase.
- Missing external lookup data does not fall back to successful hits or zero. F5 is still recorded, F4 is not incremented, and the outcome is `lookup_unavailable`. A valid lookup report is `complete`; missing, invalid, overflowing, or failed reports are `incomplete`.
- Both the vLLM worker and router now use `engine_data.kv_cache_hit`. No compatibility reader for the old key is included; upgrade frontends and workers together.
- F2–F5 need no enable flag. F1 history tracking remains separate and opt-in in #14889.

## Interpretation and limitations

- Compare the same model and phase. Prefill and decode are separate routing attempts; migration adds attempts that may include already-generated tokens. Selection and completion happen at different times.
- Multimodal routing tokens can differ from the input token IDs counted by F0.
- Existing `router_kv_hit_rate` is tier-weighted; these counters are not.
- Worker reporting is currently vLLM-only. SGLang and TensorRT-LLM KV attempts record router estimates and incomplete worker outcomes. Extending worker reporting to non-KV routing is deferred.
- Stock vLLM does not expose a separate external lookup count. Its cached-token statistics may also retain initial matches after transfer failures. F5 is a backend report, not independently verified successful reuse; backend failure-accounting work is separate.
- Check outcome coverage before interpreting F4: once a lookup series exists, later unavailable reports leave it flat rather than remove it.
- The frontend cached-token metric and its estimate fallback are unchanged.

## Validation

- After integrating upstream `main` at `6e21a3a646`, formatting and `git diff --check` passed, along with 13 focused lifecycle/worker-report/metric tests, four worker-selection tests, and four AST-isolated worker-payload tests against the resolved tree.
- The focused Rust coverage includes missing lookup versus a genuine zero, cancellation, overflow, once-only completion, and original-phase retention.
- 27 request-timing tests passed.
- Four worker-payload tests passed against the actual adapter method using AST-isolated execution; the full vLLM Python environment was not installed.
- Full `kv_router` run: 371 passed, 7 failed, 2 ignored. Failures are discovery-fixture `RecvError` failures in encoder/prefill routing, ZMQ recovery, and migration setup. One was reproduced individually; the base revision was not rebuilt, so the full suite is not claimed green.
- Rust formatting, Python syntax compilation, changed-page docs lint, Fern configuration check, and `git diff --check` passed. Python metric constants were regenerated.
- Fern broken-link checking reports one pre-existing recipe link, verified in the base revision. Ruff reports the same rule counts in the handler as the base revision; no unrelated cleanup was included.
- Rust tests used `--no-default-features`, no incremental compilation, and package test debug information disabled. No ARM image build or production deployment was performed.
- A three-frontend, two-worker H200 shadow ran a runtime-equivalent build of this tree with #14889 under mirrored production traffic and controlled cold/warm/contention/cache-churn workloads. All controlled requests completed. Current-version counters reached F0=6,233,943; F2=799,632 (12.83%); F3=795,760 (12.76%); and F4=F5=937,968 (15.05%). The workload exercised worker eviction, load-routing loss, and later worker discoveries caused by router-state lag. All three frontends and both workers contributed, and no funnel counter reset.

title: feat(router): add opt-in F1 cache reuse history
body:
## Summary: share completed history between router replicas

- When both F1 history and router replica sync are enabled, frontends share the canonical prompt and output block hashes learned from successful request completions. A frontend can now recognize blocks learned through another frontend in the same worker pool.
- Peer and local hashes use the same insertion routine. Hashing, duplicate suppression, FIFO age, byte budget, prefix lookup, and completion/metric accounting are unchanged. Peer updates do not increment request/token counters or get rebroadcast.
- Messages are scoped by worker endpoint, model, block size, and Eagle mode. Turning off router replica sync retains local-only history; turning off F1 creates no history synchronization tasks or subscriptions.
- This is best-effort sharing with bounded queues, cancellation, and reconnect backoff. There is no startup backfill. Queue/publication failures are logged. Existing FIFO eviction and missing history can still make F1 lower than F2; this change does not clamp either metric or redefine F1.

## Validation: peer-history update

- After integrating upstream `main` at `6e21a3a646`, `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `git diff --check`, and 17 focused history/lifecycle tests passed against the resolved tree.
- Native x86 Rust build and 17 focused history tests passed, including two independent histories communicating through the actual runtime event plane (default ZMQ), duplicate/FIFO equivalence, no rebroadcast, incompatible-domain rejection, bounded publication, transient setup recovery, and cancellation during retry.
- Existing completion/abort tests and five canonical output-hash tests passed. This validates history propagation, not a production rollout or new network-overhead measurement.
- Three-frontend GPU integration test passed with two Qwen3-0.6B workers, 16-token blocks, and the default ZMQ event plane. All six directed frontend pairs were exercised with distinct prefixes. After training only the source frontend, both peers imported its history without changing their request/token counters. The receiver then recognized the prefix on its first matching request: F1 was 1,248 tokens for a 1,249-token prompt, matching raw F2–F5 and the engine-reported cached-token count. All 12 requests completed; no incomplete or unavailable-lookup outcomes were recorded. This used an integration image containing this F1 change and the companion F2–F5 changes.
- A three-frontend, two-worker H200 shadow ran the runtime-equivalent peer-sharing tree at `fddb7e17bf` with the companion F2–F5 change under mirrored production traffic and controlled cold/warm/churn workloads. It processed 6,233,943 F0 tokens; all three frontends and both workers contributed, all controlled requests completed, and all funnel counters reported zero resets. At the measurement point F1 was 962,384 tokens (15.44% of F0). This validates stable peer-enabled operation and funnel behavior, not isolated publication/subscription latency.

## What this adds

F1 answers one simple question: **how many prompt tokens belong to complete blocks whose identifiers this router has seen before?** F1 is published as `dynamo_component_router_cache_loss_history_prefix_tokens_total`, with no stage label. This replaces `dynamo_component_router_cache_loss_funnel_tokens_total{stage="f1"}`. The F0 series and all accounting behavior are unchanged by the rename.

This telemetry is opt-in. `DYN_ROUTER_CACHE_REUSE_HISTORY` turns it on; it is off by default. When it is off, the router does not create the history, keep extra hashes, track generated output, or run the F1 lookup.

## Why F1 is a separate PR

F1 needs a bounded history in the router, so its review is mainly about memory use, lookup cost, and lock contention. F2–F5 use worker-reported data and have a different cost profile. Splitting F1 from #14103 lets reviewers evaluate those two overhead surfaces independently.

## How it works

- The router already computes one 64-bit identifier for each complete prompt block while choosing a worker. F1 reuses those identifiers; it does not hash the prompt a second time.
- The history is split into 64 independently locked sets. A lookup touches only the set for that block, so unrelated lookups can proceed in parallel.
- A global first-in, first-out queue decides which old identifiers to evict when the byte budget is full.
- Each identifier is stored once. Seeing a duplicate neither inserts it again nor makes it newer.
- Reads do not take the queue lock. When a request finishes, it first checks the 64 sets; only identifiers that appear new require the queue lock, followed by a second check before insertion.
- To continue identifying generated blocks, the request keeps only the unfinished tail of the prompt and the relevant hashing options. It does not copy the full prompt.
- `DYN_ROUTER_CACHE_REUSE_HISTORY_BYTES` sets the history budget. The default is 256 MiB for each independent KV router/indexer history, enough for an estimated 8,388,608 distinct identifiers using the conservative 32-byte planning estimate.

## What happens to a request

- A complete, valid response records F0 and F1 exactly once and then adds its block identifiers to history.
- An aborted request, stream error, cancellation, or dropped connection records exactly one incomplete observation and does **not** add anything to history.

## Test and overhead results

### Functional validation on ARM

| Test | Result | What it establishes |
|---|---|---|
| Tiny-model exact-count test | Three 484-token inputs produced `F0=1,452`, `F1=960`, 3 complete observations, 0 incomplete observations, populated history gauges, and no F2–F5 series | F1 accounting and stage isolation are correct on the target architecture |
| Real mirrored-traffic shadow | `F0=13.22M`, `F1=0.903M` (6.83%), no F2–F5 series, zero request errors, and zero process restarts | The feature operates stably under real traffic |

### Lookup microbenchmark

The release-build benchmark uses the same 64-set lookup and FIFO behavior as this PR, with the history filled to 8.39 million entries. It ran locally on x86; it is not a target-host latency measurement.

| Block size | Complete blocks checked | F1 lookup | Share of 156.9 µs router work |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 12,288 (current) | 4 | 0.100 µs | 0.06% |
| 1,536 (planned) | 34 | 1.00 µs | 0.64% |
| 128 (stress case) | 417 | 13.7 µs | 8.7% |
| 64 (stress case) | 834 | 31.4 µs | 20.0% |

### Measured router throughput

This release-mode Rust benchmark sends prebuilt requests through the real in-process `RoutingHost::generate` path. It includes KV worker scoring, exact admitted dispatch, response-stream finalization, and F1 completion accounting. A fixed fake discovery snapshot supplies workers and an immediate backend removes HTTP, NATS, and model execution.

The table is the 26-worker, concurrency-one, duplicate-heavy case: 10,000 measured requests after 1,000 warmups. Each result is the median of six runs split across opposite off/on orders on two pinned x86 logical CPUs.

| Block size | Blocks | Throughput off → on | Change | Route p50 off → on | Route p95 off → on | Route p99 off → on | CPU/request change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 12,288 (current) | 4 | 32,636 → 32,594 req/s | -0.13% | 26.15 → 26.67 µs | 35.41 → 35.35 µs | 46.40 → 45.03 µs | +1.1% |
| 1,536 (planned) | 34 | 31,229 → 29,730 req/s | -4.80% | 27.56 → 28.90 µs | 38.24 → 39.55 µs | 49.67 → 49.79 µs | +3.3% |
| 128 (stress) | 417 | 22,785 → 18,577 req/s | -18.47% | 38.78 → 43.63 µs | 52.98 → 57.20 µs | 65.02 → 70.65 µs | +20.8% |
| 64 (stress) | 834 | 16,761 → 12,553 req/s | -25.10% | 53.25 → 63.22 µs | 69.77 → 79.01 µs | 95.09 → 105.59 µs | +32.2% |

The full 48-cell sweep also covered concurrency 1/8/32, 26/1,000 workers, and duplicate-heavy/all-new traffic. At 1,000 workers, existing worker scoring dominates: the planned 34-block throughput change ranged from +0.69% to -2.76% across the six concurrency/workload cells. The current four-block shape ranged from +1.26% to -5.08%; that spread, including apparent wins, is the local noise envelope rather than evidence that F1 improves throughput.

### Completion pressure and retention

Duplicate-only completions bypassed the FIFO exactly as designed: after 11,000 repeated requests, enabled histories retained only 4/34/417/834 identifiers. All-new runs retained exactly `(warmup + measured requests) × blocks` until capacity.

The best F1-on all-new rates observed through the real 26-worker router path were 28,139 completions/s (112,558 new blocks/s) at 4 blocks, 23,568/s (801,316 blocks/s) at 34 blocks, 7,937/s (3.31M blocks/s) at 417 blocks, and 4,761/s (3.97M blocks/s) at 834 blocks. These include all router lifecycle work and are not isolated FIFO ceilings.

The direct completion microbenchmark remains useful as a lock-pressure bound: 210.5k/31.7k/3.09k/1.56k all-new completions/s at 4/34/417/834 blocks. Current Kimi traffic adds about 1.55 new identifiers/s, orders of magnitude below either measurement.

At that observed new-identifier rate, the default history is modeled to retain about 62.8 days with the current 12,288-token block size. If the rate grows linearly with the planned 8× increase in block count, modeled retention is 7.85 days at 1,536 tokens. These are estimates, not direct long-duration measurements.


## Limitations

- The earlier F1-only mirrored run was saturated and severely imbalanced across workers. The newer three-frontend shadow validates peer-enabled stability and varied funnel behavior, but it still does not isolate publication/subscription latency overhead.
- No isolated F1 timer was collected on the target ARM host. The lookup microbenchmark and router-throughput harness ran locally on x86; they are not target-ARM serving-QPS measurements.

## Where reviewers should start

- `lib/llm/src/kv_router/cache_history.rs`: the 64 sets, byte limit, insertion, and eviction behavior.
- `lib/llm/src/kv_router/routing_host/kv.rs`: reuse of the block identifiers already computed during routing.
- `lib/llm/src/kv_router/routing_host/request_guard.rs`: exactly-once completion/incomplete accounting and generated-block tracking.

## Related issue

- Split from #14103.

## Validation

Metric-name revision: all 8 tests in the metric-names Rust module passed using an isolated `rustc --test` build against cached dependencies. Regenerated the Python constants and verified the new constant. Changed-file rustfmt and `git diff --check` passed. No full LLM rebuild or new shadow rollout for this naming-only revision.

title: refactor(replay): delegate Weka ingestion to AISimulate
body:
#### Summary

Replace Dynamo's duplicate Weka parser and converter with AISimulate's graph loader. Keep `trace_format="weka"` as a compatibility adapter and execute the resulting graph through the existing typed agentic replay path.

- Remove the Dynamo Weka parser, lowering code, converter binary, and their build targets.
- Preserve source block sizes, explicit nested timestamp overrides, and the resolved timestamp basis in offline/online summaries and runner metadata.
- Retain source-model provenance and the configured execution target; adapt to the required AISimulate API changes.
- Keep the router implementation unchanged apart from the new protocol field required by AISimulate.

#### Weka behavior changes

- `auto` selects one nested timestamp basis for the whole corpus. Adding a relative-timestamp witness can change other files' interpretation. The resolved basis is reported; explicit `absolute` retains before-marker rejection.
- `out: 0` remains zero, replacing the former `max(1, out)` normalization; output totals and timing/throughput metrics can change.
- Missing/null `api_time` remains absent in provenance; dependency classification uses a zero-duration interval instead of rejecting the input.

title: test(operator): stop pinning encoding/json's incidental struct name
body:
## Overview:

Stop asserting an `encoding/json` implementation detail in a webhook
validation test, so `make envtest`/`make test` doesn't spuriously fail under
a Go 1.27 toolchain even though `go.mod` only requires `go 1.26.6`.

## Details:

`assertAdmissionErrors` in `suite_envtest_test.go` already normalizes two
incidental substrings (`Invalid value: "object": ` / `"array": `) before
comparing rendered error messages. This adds the same kind of normalization
for the leading Go struct type name `json.UnmarshalTypeError` prints ahead
of the field path (`Go struct field <Type>.spec...`). Which struct that name
is depends on the JSON engine: with jsonv2 (Go 1.27's default) it is always
the outermost struct passed to `json.Unmarshal`; on Go 1.26.6 (what `go.mod`
declares and CI runs) it is the struct that *declares* the erroring field,
so it changes with nesting depth. Either way it carries no information the
field path doesn't already carry, and it differs between the two engines
for the byte-identical input.

The normalizing regex matches `[^\s.]*` rather than `\S+?` for the type
name, because `\S+?` requires at least one character and so deletes the
first path segment whenever encoding/json prints an *empty* type name —
which jsonv2 does whenever the unmarshal target isn't a pointer to a named
type, and Go 1.26 does for an anonymous struct's field.

The assertion is now a function of the field path made of struct fields —
not of paths through list indexes or map keys, which are a separate,
pre-existing case this test does not exercise. The
`malformed provider override field is invalid without echoing its value`
row also gained a `notWantErr: "rack"` check, so it actually verifies the
property its name claims (true for this specific input; a
`validateKnownGroveShape` denial can echo the submitted value for other
inputs, e.g. an invalid duration or timestamp — a separate, pre-existing
issue this PR does not touch).

**Validation — negative control, the test fails without the fix:**
Reverting the two changed test files to their state before this PR
(production code untouched) and re-running the one affected subtest under
a Go 1.27.0 toolchain:

```
without the fix: 0 passed, 1 failed
with the fix:    1 passed, 0 failed
```

- Re-ran the full `internal/webhook/validation` package under both Go 1.26.6
  and Go 1.27.0 after the fix: both `ok` (467 passed, 0 failed), no other
  test affected. No behavior change to `internal/provideroverride` — this
  is a test-only assertion fix.
- `go vet ./internal/webhook/validation/...` and `gofmt -l` clean.

## Where should the reviewer start?

`suite_envtest_test.go`'s `assertAdmissionErrors` (the `goStructFieldType`
normalization) and the updated expectation plus `notWantErr` addition in
`dynamographdeployment_validation_envtest_test.go`.

## Related Issues

**🔗 This PR is linked to an issue:**
- Closes #14128

title: feat(vllm): add external encoder handoff
body:
## Why

Dynamo already maintains the `VisionEncoderBackend` framework, but applications that place the encoder outside the aggregated vLLM worker still had to reimplement image extraction, encoder driving, tensor packing, request sanitization, and the decoder-side prompt reconstruction contract.

This PR makes that handoff a vLLM-owned contract while keeping `GenerateRequest.encoder_result` opaque in `dynamo.common`.

## User contract

```python
handoff = ExternalEncoderHandoff(backend)
handoff.load(model_id)
prepared = await handoff.prepare_request(request, target_model=generator_model)
handoff.shutdown()
```

Users implement `VisionEncoderBackend`; Dynamo owns the rest of the external handoff.

## What changed

- Add public `ExternalEncoderHandoff` lifecycle and request-preparation API.
- Move the concrete versioned wire format under the vLLM custom-encoder component.
- Share one linear prompt builder between inline and external encoder paths.
- Sanitize source-side multimodal state before forwarding to stock aggregated `dynamo.vllm`.
- Keep decoder-side conflict validation and off-event-loop tensor reconstruction.

Version 0 remains intentionally narrow: image inputs, ordered two-dimensional CPU linear embeddings, MsgPack request-plane transport, token-in/token-out, and a text-only aggregated vLLM worker with `--enable-prompt-embeds`.

The thin application-owned example is #14859.

## Test plan

- Unit coverage for payload validation and round trips, artifact ordering, request sanitization, lifecycle, malformed inputs, and inline/external prompt parity.
- Existing handler coverage for aggregated, text-mode rejection, and conditional-bypass behavior.
- Pre-commit and Python syntax compilation pass locally.

title: feat: K3 structural tag default
body: ## Summary This is the activation and integration half of a coordinated change addressing two tool-calling correctness problems: 1. **Kimi K3 needed stronger model-native guidance.** The companion [frontend-crates#196](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/frontend-crates/pull/196) hardens the K3 XTML grammar used after an automatic call begins. 2. **Supported models were not receiving structural guidance by default.** Dynamo previously defaulted structural tags to disabled with conditional `auto` activation. Consequently, ordinary `tool_choice="auto"` requests with omitted `strict` remained unconstrained even when the configured parser had a validated structural-tag builder. This PR enables structural guidance by default for supported parsers, aligns the Rust and Python frontend policies, and preserves non-failing compatibility fallbacks for unsupported parsers and schemas. ## Default policy | Setting | Previous default | New default | |---|---|---| | `DYN_ENABLE_STRUCTURAL_TAG` | `false` | `true` | | `DYN_STRUCTURAL_TAG_SCOPE` | `auto` | `always` | | `DYN_STRUCTURAL_TAG_SCHEMA` | `auto` | `auto` | The `auto` schema mode now means: - omitted `strict` or `strict:true`: use the declared parameter schema; - explicit `strict:false`: constrain the native tool envelope but relax the argument schema; - `DYN_STRUCTURAL_TAG_SCHEMA=strict`: use the declared schema for every tool, overriding `strict:false`. Automatic tool choice remains optional. Structural guidance does not make the model call a tool; it constrains the output only if the model starts the model-native tool-call format. ## Request processing and fallback ```mermaid flowchart TD A[OpenAI request with tools] --> B{Structural tags enabled?} B -- No --> F[Existing compatibility path] B -- Yes --> C{tool_choice} C -- none --> N[Rust exclusion tag or existing Python none handling] C -- auto, required, or named --> D{Configured parser can build a tag?} D -- No --> F D -- Yes --> E{Tool strict value} E -- omitted or true --> G[Native envelope plus declared argument schema] E -- false --> H[Native envelope plus relaxed arguments] G --> I[Send structural tag to backend guided decoding] H --> I D -- Build unsupported or fails --> F ``` The policy is capability-based: it uses the existing parser registry and builder configuration. This PR does not add or change model-to-parser mappings. When no builder exists, or a builder cannot safely produce a structural tag, Dynamo falls back instead of introducing a new request error: - automatic tool choice returns to existing best-effort generation; - ordinary required or named choices retain their existing guided-JSON fallback where applicable; and - Kimi's marker-delimited forced choices retain their native prompt/parser fallback rather than receiving an incompatible generic JSON grammar. Explicitly disabling structural tags is authoritative. ```bash python3 -m dynamo.vllm ... --no-dyn-enable-structural-tag python3 -m dynamo.sglang ... --no-dyn-enable-structural-tag ``` Equivalent environment setting: ```bash DYN_ENABLE_STRUCTURAL_TAG=false ``` `strict:false` is only an argument-schema opt-out; it does not disable the model-native tool envelope. Operators that want the previous conditional activation policy can set: ```bash DYN_STRUCTURAL_TAG_SCOPE=auto ``` With that scope, required and named choices remain eligible, while automatic choice is activated only for explicit `strict:true` or `parallel_tool_calls:false`. ## Frontend and sidecar behavior The same mode, scope, and schema decisions are applied by: - Rust frontend preprocessing; - Python vLLM frontend preprocessing; and - Python SGLang frontend preprocessing. The Python paths share a small policy helper while retaining backend-specific grammar construction and response handling. Native Rust sidecars retain their existing conservative `off`/`auto` runtime configuration and are not included in this default change. This prevents a sidecar from receiving unsupported structural guidance merely because the regular worker defaults changed. For `tool_choice="none"`, Rust preprocessing can install parser-specific token exclusions. Python vLLM and SGLang retain their existing prompt and response shaping; this PR does not add token banning to those paths. ## Affected parsers The Rust parser registry currently exposes structural-tag builders for: - `hermes` and `qwen25`; - `qwen3_coder` and `nemotron_nano`; - `deepseek_v3_2` and `deepseek_v4`; - `kimi_k2`, `kimi_k3`, and `kimi-k3`; and - `inkling`. Other Rust parsers, including currently tested Mistral and Gemma paths, continue through compatibility fallback. Python vLLM and SGLang support is determined by the parser implementation in the installed engine version. It can therefore differ from the Rust registry, but unsupported combinations still fall back without rejecting the request. ## Correctness validation Validated results include: - Nemotron schema correctness: `639/700 = 91.3%` to `698/700 = 99.7%`, with 100% schema validity among emitted calls; - Mistral with Python SGLang: `24/54 = 44.4%` to `42/54 = 77.8%`; - Gemma with Python SGLang: `78/90 = 86.7%` to `84/90 = 93.3%`; - Qwen through the Rust frontend on vLLM and SGLang: unchanged at `48/48`, with the schema matrix unchanged at `30/30`; and - unsupported Mistral and Gemma Rust builders: exact default-on/forced-off equivalence, confirming compatibility fallback. The graph deliberately reports the validated frontend/parser combination for each model; it does not imply that every engine version exposes the same Python parser capabilities. ## Performance validation At concurrency 8, the measured p50 TTFT values were close: | Model/path | Without PR | With PR | |---|---:|---:| | Nemotron | 164.73 ms | 160.84 ms | | DeepSeek V4 Flash | 243.52 ms | 241.48 ms | | Gemma 4 unsupported-builder fallback | 158.03 ms | 156.86 ms | These small differences are treated as equivalence, not as evidence that structural guidance improves inference speed. The clean DeepSeek run used balanced default-on/off blocks, and the Gemma fallback run confirmed that the capability check adds no material serving overhead when no builder exists. ## Code validation Focused Rust and Python tests cover: - the new CLI and environment defaults; - authoritative global opt-out; - `always` and legacy `auto` activation scopes; - omitted, true, and false request strictness; - automatic, required, named, and none tool choices; - supported-builder selection; - unsupported parser and schema fallback; - preservation of generic forced-tool fallback; - native Kimi forced-choice fallback; and - policy parity between Python vLLM and Python SGLang preprocessing. ## Dependency The Kimi K3 grammar and shared structural-tag schema behavior are supplied by [ai-dynamo/frontend-crates#196](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/frontend-crates/pull/196). ## Summary by CodeRabbit - **New Features** - Structural tags are now enabled by default with an `always` scope. - Tool schemas enforce declared constraints by default; explicit `strict=false` remains unconstrained. - Added consistent structural-tag support across Rust, vLLM, and SGLang preprocessing. - **Bug Fixes** - Invalid forced tool choices now return clear validation errors. - Unsupported structural-tag construction falls back to compatible JSON or unconstrained guidance. - **Documentation** - Updated runtime configuration and tool-calling guidance with new defaults and backend behavior. - **Tests** - Expanded coverage for activation policies, strictness, fallbacks, parser compatibility, and configuration propagation.

title: feat(mocker): add a TensorRT-LLM OpenEngine mocker server
body:
> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Stacked on #14349** and targets that branch, so the diff here is only the mocker. It cannot build against `main` until #14349 merges — the crate is written against `openengine.v1`, which that PR introduces. Please review #14349 first.

## Summary

Dynamo has wire-protocol mocker servers for vLLM and SGLang, but not for TensorRT-LLM. Without one, `lib/sidecar/trtllm` can only be exercised against canned in-process fakes or a real GPU engine — so nothing in CI runs the *real* sidecar against realistic KV capacity, batching, admission control, and prefill/decode timing. That gap is what made the disaggregation bugs found during the OpenEngine work (endpoint mangling, stale-session hangs) expensive to catch.

`dynamo-trtllm-mocker-server` implements `openengine.v1` on top of the Mocker scheduler, so the unmodified `dynamo-trtllm-sidecar` connects to it as if it were a real engine, with no GPU. `EngineType::Trtllm` already existed in `dynamo-mocker` (vLLM scheduler core plus the `guaranteed_no_evict` admission policy); only the wire server was missing.

Layout mirrors the two existing siblings — `lib/mocker/servers/{vllm,sglang}` — so the three read as a set.

## Why the handoff validation is strict

The sidecar relays `attributes_struct` through a JSON codec whose realistic failure modes — a dropped field defaulting to empty, a coerced number type, a flattened list — all still produce a *plausible* session. Presence checks alone would not notice. So the prefill role stamps four attributes that each pin one distinct hazard (a string, a whole-valued double, a deliberately fractional double, a list), and the decode role requires them back in their original JSON types.

The decode role also **replays the context phase's first token**, so both legs' token accounting matches a real engine's rather than the decode leg inventing a fresh stream.

## Deliberate: KV events return UNIMPLEMENTED

`GetKvEventSources` and `SubscribeKvEvents` refuse, matching what the real TensorRT-LLM server does today. A mocker that answered them would let a KV-routing test pass here and fail in production. A test guards the refusal so it isn't "helpfully" filled in later. The consequence — **Dynamo KV routing cannot be exercised against this mocker** — is stated in the README; use the worker-level `dynamo.mocker` for that.

## Canonical-layer moves

`deterministic_token_id` moves into `dynamo_mocker::live` rather than becoming a third private copy, with `deterministic_output_tokens` expressed in terms of it. The sidecar's disaggregation constants (`REQUEST_TYPE_KEY`, `CONTEXT_ONLY`, `context_only_extra`) are exported so the wire contract has one definition instead of four.

## Validation

**Tests** — 25 unit + 6 integration. The integration tests drive the *real* `TrtllmSidecarEngine` over a real socket, including a full prefill→decode round trip across two server processes, and assert on requests the server received, not only on replies.

Every fix in this PR was mutation-tested — the fix was reverted and the matching test confirmed to fail. Five of six mutations were caught. The sixth is not: reverting the `aborted` check inside the terminal branch leaves the suite green. With the `cancel()` fix in place that branch only covers a narrow race (engine emits `completed` before the scheduler releases the route) that I could not construct deterministically. It's kept as defense-in-depth with no test behind it.

`cargo clippy --all-targets` and the full pre-commit suite pass.

**End to end, CPU only** — frontend → sidecar → mocker, aggregated and disaggregated. Disaggregated confirmed genuinely split via distinct `prefill_worker_id`/`decode_worker_id` in the frontend logs.

**Load** — AIPerf 0.12.0, ISL 136 / OSL 128, streaming, 8,600+ requests, zero errors. With `speedup_ratio: 1000` the simulated engine is ~free, so this measures the Dynamo path itself:

| Conc | req/s | out tok/s | Latency avg | p99 | TTFT avg |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 22.0 | 2,817 | 44.0 ms | 45.1 | 32.1 ms |
| 32 | 533.5 | 68,293 | 56.3 | 93.1 | 6.4 |
| 128 | 1,013.6 | 127,403 | 119.3 | 178.2 | 25.5 |
| 256 | 1,041.7 | 132,671 | 225.0 | 296.3 | 39.0 |

The knee is at 128 — 128→256 buys 2.8% throughput for 89% more latency. Disaggregated costs ~4% throughput at concurrency 32 and ~12% at 128 (routing only; no KV transfer is simulated). Debug binaries, so absolute numbers are pessimistic; the shape is the point.

**One thing worth chasing separately:** concurrency 1 has *worse* TTFT than concurrency 32 (32.1 ms vs 6.4 ms), and the distribution is bimodal — `min 2.85 ms, p50 43.65 ms` — with the ~40 ms cluster vanishing as soon as traffic is continuous. That is the signature of Nagle interacting with delayed-ACK on an idle connection, but I have **not** confirmed it; it would want a `TCP_NODELAY` check on the frontend→sidecar request plane. If real, it is a single-stream latency issue that load testing hides. Not introduced by this PR.

title: fix(router): propagate client cancellation to remote prefill workers
body:
## Summary

In disaggregated SGLang serving, a client disconnect before the first token could stop at Dynamo’s routing boundary while remote prefill, decode bootstrap, and KV handoff work continued. This change propagates the terminal request context to the selected remote prefill worker only when both SGLang worker legs advertise the versioned cancellation guarantee, closing the leak without changing behavior for older, mixed-version, vLLM, or TensorRT-LLM deployments.

## What was broken

The router dispatched remote prefill work without linking it to the client request context. When the client disconnected before any output was returned, the parent request stopped but the selected prefill worker and decode-side bootstrap receiver could remain alive, retaining admission and KV-transfer state and delaying follow-up requests. Propagating cancellation unconditionally would also be unsafe because older or mixed workers do not guarantee cancellation at every handoff phase.

## How it was fixed

Compatible SGLang workers advertise `DISAGG_PREFILL_CANCEL_ANYTIME_V1`, and the router enables propagation only when both the selected prefill and decode legs provide that capability. The linked lifecycle preserves stop-to-kill escalation without downgrading an already killed context, remains active through bootstrap draining and prefill stream consumption, and uses the internal engine request ID to abort registered work while completing bounded stream and admission cleanup. Missing or stale capability metadata fails closed.

## Details

- gate context propagation on paired decode and selected-prefill capability metadata
- preserve registration-before-dispatch ordering and propagate stop/kill state without ever downgrading a killed context
- fail closed for mixed-version or missing capability metadata
- preserve bootstrap draining, admission release, and KV cleanup
- add paired-capability, admission-release, and two-GPU NATS/TCP regression coverage

## Stack

- Decode lifecycle: #14781 (merged)
- Prefill lifecycle: #14782 (merged)
- Router propagation: this PR

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C[Client] --> F[Dynamo frontend]
    F --> R[KV-aware router]
    R --> S[Select remote prefill worker]
    S --> G{Both SGLang legs advertise cancellation capability?}
    D[Decode worker metadata] --> G
    P[Selected prefill metadata] --> G
    G -- Yes --> L[Link parent and selected prefill contexts]
    G -- Missing or mixed --> N[Dispatch without context propagation]
    L --> W[Selected prefill worker]
    N --> W
    W --> E[SGLang prefill engine]
    W --> B[Bootstrap and KV handoff]
    B --> D
    R --> A[Admission and bootstrap guard]
```

## Sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant F as Frontend
    participant R as Router
    participant M as Worker metadata
    participant P as Selected prefill worker
    participant E as SGLang engine
    C->>F: Submit request
    F->>R: Route request
    R->>M: Select prefill and read both capabilities
    alt Both SGLang legs support cancellation
        R->>P: Dispatch with linked request context
        P->>E: Generate with internal request ID
        P-->>R: Return bootstrap metadata
        C--xF: Disconnect before first output
        F-->>R: Parent context reaches a terminal state
        alt Parent is already killed
            R-->>P: Propagate kill immediately
        else Parent stops generating
            R-->>P: Propagate stop
            R-->>P: Propagate a later kill, if observed
        end
        P->>E: Abort registered request
        P-->>R: Finish and release admission state
    else Capability is missing or mixed
        R->>P: Dispatch without context propagation
    end
```

## Where should the reviewer start?

- `lib/llm/src/kv_router/prefill_router/mod.rs` for worker selection and propagation gating
- `lib/llm/src/kv_router/prefill_router/cancellation.rs` for linked-context ownership and escalation
- `lib/llm/src/discovery/model_manager.rs` for paired capability checks
- `tests/fault_tolerance/cancellation/test_sglang.py` for the real two-GPU regression

## Validation

- 361 affected Python tests passed at the previous exact full stacked head
- 100 focused cancellation and frontend-decoding tests passed after the final CI repair and rebase
- focused mypy validation passes for the cancellation module
- 5 focused Rust cancellation tests passed after the final cleanup and rebase
- all touched-file pre-commit hooks passed
- thermo-nuclear code-quality review approved
- fresh independent Claude Opus 5 review with a 1M context window found no P0/P1 issues; validated P2 findings were fixed in `1b213a4d7e`
- current head `1b213a4d7e`: 18 prefill-router Rust tests passed, Python syntax checks passed, all touched-file pre-commit hooks passed, and every commit is GitHub-verified
- pre-review exact-head two-GPU CI at `213dd4446c` on NVIDIA L40S hardware: 9 selected tests passed, including decode cancellation and both `prefill_received` and `decode_handoff` phases over NATS and TCP
- controlled two-GPU A/B on NVIDIA GB200 hardware with SGLang 0.5.19 and Qwen3-0.6B:
  - pre-fix parent 35259ac0d6bf8d959581e3ccb1f239440f6b5b71: the request reached prefill, the client disconnected before first output, and no matching prefill abort appeared within 15 seconds; 1 failed in 302.15s at the intended assertion
  - fixed source 4a21bfd631d05c9a0c200a54db7af10cd526b788 over NATS: 1 passed in 276.69s
  - fixed source 4a21bfd631d05c9a0c200a54db7af10cd526b788 over TCP: 1 passed in 275.30s
  - both fixed runs observed the remote prefill abort and then served a follow-up request through the same prefill/decode pair

## Related Issues

Closes #13691

title: feat(operator): allow EPP replicas in Dynamo mode
body:
> [!NOTE]
> Targets a later release, not 1.5.0. #14756 documents the single-replica limit as it stands in 1.5.0 and should land on its own; this PR changes that behaviour for a subsequent release.
## Summary

The EPP in the standalone mode allows replication but the EPP in the dynamo mode only allowed replica 1. This PR addresses this limitation. 

Prior to this PR Admission was rejected any EPP component with `replicas` other than 1, so the endpoint picker could neither scale for throughput nor survive the loss of its pod. That restriction was not justified by a router limitation. The Frontend hosts the same KV router and allows for replication:

This PR does not introduce any new impresisions. It extends the current frontEnd behavior to the EPP in the dynamo mode. 

- **Prefix-cache state needs no synchronization.** Workers publish KV events to the event plane and every subscriber receives all of them (plain NATS `subscribe`, not `queue_subscribe`), so each replica builds an equivalent radix tree. Cache-overlap scoring, which dominates worker choice on prefix-heavy traffic, stays as accurate with N replicas as with one.
- **Active-sequence state is shared by `DYN_ROUTER_REPLICA_SYNC`**, IF ENABLED just like in the frontEnd,  which reaches the EPP's decode and prefill routers through `try_kv_router_config_from_dynamo_env` and runs the same `ActiveSequencesMultiWorker` replica sync the Frontend uses.
- The load count will also be off just like with the FrontEnd replication.
- The freeing of a Booking is also supported in EPP. 

### Changes

- Remove the `EPP component must have exactly 1 replica` admission rule.
- Leave `DYN_ROUTER_REPLICA_SYNC` off by default, matching the Frontend-hosted router. Sharing does not divide as replicas are added: a replica receives events for every request the fleet routes, not just its own, and an `add` carries one block hash per KV block of its prompt. Document when turning it on is worth the volume instead of choosing for the deployment.
- Document the accuracy cost in the Gateway API routing reference.

### Documented accuracy shortfall

The reference now covers the limit that is specific to the EPP rather than inherited from the router. The Frontend owns a request end to end and frees its booking when the work ends. The EPP only selects but  Envoy dispatches. The Consequences at more than one replica:

- A retry can land on a different EPP:
     1. Request R comes in. Envoy asks EPP A. A says "send it to W1" and notes W1 busy with R.                                                                                 
     2. W1 starts generating.                                                                                                                                                  
     3. The Envoy/EPP-A conversation breaks , i.e. pod restart, timeout, network blip.                                                                                              
     4. A sees the conversation end, assumes R finished, tears up the note. But W1 is still                                                                                    
     generating.                                                                                                                                                            
     5. Envoy retries R and this time asks EPP-B, which knows nothing about attempt 1 and books a                                                                              
     worker fresh. 
- An `ext_proc` disconnect does not cancel dispatched work, so the EPP stops accounting for a request still consuming KV blocks.
- The reaper at `DYN_ROUTER_ACTIVE_REQUEST_EXPIRY_SECS` (default 300s) bounds the error without correcting it, and lease expiry is local and publishes no `free`.

The effect is a transient over- or under-estimate of one worker's active load, on some replicas and not others. It shifts load balancing, not correctness. The selection-to-booking race and the never-synchronized output-block growth are documented alongside it, with guidance on choosing a replica count.

In essence both EPP modes have the same accuracy issue. What differs is who owns the transport and the peer discovery:

| | Standalone | Dynamo mode |
|---|---|---|
| Enabled by | `DYN_EPP_PEER_SERVICE` + `POD_IP` | `DYN_ROUTER_REPLICA_SYNC=true`, off by default and set through `podTemplate` env |
| Transport | ZMQ sockets the EPP binds itself, on `DYN_EPP_REPLICA_SYNC_PORT` (default 9092), topic `dynamo.slot-tracker.v1` | The Dynamo event plane, addressed and discovered by the runtime. ZMQ-backed by default, NATS when the runtime is configured for it |
| Peers | An explicit endpoint list the EPP maintains from its own Service's EndpointSlices | No Kubernetes watch. Publishers come from Dynamo discovery |
| Kubernetes RBAC | `services:get` and `endpointslices:list/watch` | None |

Both normally speak ZMQ — `EventTransportKind::Zmq` is the default and direct-ZMQ active-sequence ingress is enabled by default — so the difference is ownership, not protocol. Standalone binds its own sockets and maintains its own peer list, which is the only reason that mode needs Kubernetes permissions for replication at all. A Dynamo-mode EPP hands the events to the runtime and never learns who its peers are.

## Validation

- `go test ./...` in `deploy/operator` — 42 packages pass, no failures.
- Admission tests cover both paths: a native Rust EPP accepts more than one replica, and a legacy Go EPP still requires exactly one.
- Updated the envtest case that asserted rejection of `replicas: 2` to assert acceptance, and the field-path test that pinned `spec.components[].replicas` among the EPP validator's emitted paths.
- `python3 docs/fern/scripts/docs_lint.py --scan docs` — 0 errors (8 pre-existing warnings on untouched files).
- `fern check` / `fern docs broken-links` not run: the CLI is not installed locally.

The magnitude of the selection-to-booking race at realistic arrival rates needs measurement.

## Related Issues

**🚫 This PR is NOT linked to an issue**:
- [x] Confirmed — no related issue

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

  * EPP deployments can now run with multiple replicas instead of being limited to a single replica.
  * Native Rust EPP deployments automatically enable replica synchronization when multiple replicas are configured, while allowing explicit configuration overrides.
  * Replica settings are now applied consistently across deployments.

* **Documentation**

title: feat(router): ship opt-in soft affinity load guard
body:
## Summary

Ship an opt-in soft session-affinity worker-selection policy in the built-in catalog. When a parent-group binding has an eligible target, the policy keeps that worker until its active-request count exceeds `max_active_requests` and another eligible worker is lower by at least `move_margin`. Dynamo's existing affinity coordinator continues to own and update the binding; this PR adds no parent-key logic or router CLI flag.

For example, with `max_active_requests: 7` and `move_margin: 2`, source/alternative loads of 7/0 and 8/7 retain the source, while 8/6 selects the alternative. The shipped defaults are 32/2. The policy is selected through existing router-policy YAML.

The existing `soft-pin-repin` example requires a custom catalog build and moves once the threshold is crossed even when the alternative is equally or more loaded. This proposal makes the guarded behavior available in a stock build. It is separate from #15139's binary retain/ignore soft-target switch and #14596's generic two-tier cache/load weights.

## Validation

- `cargo test --locked -p dynamo-custom-policy-builtin`: 11 passed.
- `cargo clippy --locked -p dynamo-custom-policy-builtin --all-targets -- -D warnings`: passed.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` and `git diff --check`: passed.
- Fern docs lint: 0 errors; 8 warnings in untouched files.
- The three touched upstream files matched current main's blob hashes before publication.

## Limits and next validation

This is a **draft capability PR**, not a measured speedup. Active-request count is a coarse load proxy; the policy does not know hotspot duration or cache residency. Unbound requests choose the least-loaded eligible worker without consulting cache overlap. Historical GPU measurements motivate the question but used an earlier router revision.

Before requesting merge, compare this policy on current main against hard affinity, two-tier with its existing tunable thresholds, and applicable soft-affinity configuration. Use equal capacity, two physical GPUs, balanced source/order, short and sustained hotspots, plus explicit stay/move controls. Report group-max TTFT, request latency, cached/computed tokens, placement, background impact, and failures. Keep unfavorable valid samples and stop if existing configuration already covers the workload or this policy regresses short hotspots.

## Where should the reviewer start?

Review `lib/router-plugins/builtin/src/soft_affinity_load_guard.rs` for the threshold and margin decisions, then `lib/router-plugins/builtin/src/lib.rs` for registration and YAML resolution.

## Related issues

Relates to #14536. Builds on merged #14521.
