title: fix(responses): preserve raw reasoning_content without an explicit summary request
body:
## Overview:

Dynamo's Responses API converter silently drops non-empty backend `reasoning_content` whenever the request did not set `reasoning.summary`, even though the raw-reasoning event/output-item lifecycle it builds does not actually depend on summary mode. This PR removes that gate so reasoning is preserved whenever the backend returns it.

## Details:

- `lib/llm/src/protocols/openai/responses/mod.rs`: removed the `reasoning_summary_requested()` gate from the non-streaming reasoning-conversion path (`chat_completion_to_response`), and removed the now-unused `reasoning_summary_requested()` helper.
- `lib/llm/src/protocols/openai/responses/stream_converter.rs`: removed the equivalent gate from the streaming conversion path (`ResponseStreamConverter::append_chunk_events`).
- Updated the two existing tests that had locked in the old (gate-on) behavior to assert the corrected behavior, mirroring the assertions already used by the adjacent, already-passing "summary requested" test cases, since the fix makes both code paths identical regardless of whether `reasoning.summary` was requested.

## Where should the reviewer start?

`lib/llm/src/protocols/openai/responses/mod.rs` around line 1159 (non-streaming) and `lib/llm/src/protocols/openai/responses/stream_converter.rs` around line 411 (streaming) — these are the two gate removals the issue points at directly.

## Related Issues

**🔗 This PR is linked to an issue:**
Closes #14069

## Summary

- Backend `reasoning_content` is now surfaced as a `ReasoningItem` (raw `content`, empty `summary`) whenever the backend returns it, for both `/v1/responses` streaming and non-streaming paths, regardless of whether the request set `reasoning.summary`.
- Removed the now-dead `ResponseParams::reasoning_summary_requested()` helper (no remaining callers after the gate removal).

## Validation

- `cargo test -p dynamo-llm --lib --no-default-features protocols::openai::responses::` (run with `CARGO_PROFILE_TEST_DEBUG=0` to fit the local build machine's memory): **107 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored**, including both rewritten regression tests:
  - `stream_converter::tests::test_reasoning_without_requested_summary_still_streams_raw_reasoning ... ok`
  - `tests::test_reasoning_text_preserved_without_explicit_summary_request ... ok`
- `cargo check -p dynamo-llm --lib` and `--tests` (default features, i.e. including `block-manager`/CUDA/NIXL): both pass cleanly with no errors, so the change also type-checks under the default feature set used by CI.
- Confirmed via `grep -rn` across `lib/` that `reasoning_summary_requested()` had exactly two call sites before this change (one per file) and no other references anywhere, so removing both gates and the helper itself leaves no dangling references.

Fixes #14069.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **Bug Fixes**
  - Preserved non-empty reasoning content in Responses API results, even when no reasoning summary was explicitly requested.
  - Ensured streamed reasoning content produces the appropriate reasoning events and remains available in the output.

<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

#### Context cost of preserving raw reasoning

Per review: once raw `reasoning_content` is always surfaced as a `ReasoningItem`, a caller that feeds the assistant's prior output back in as input for a follow-up turn (the standard multi-turn `Item::Reasoning` echo path) is echoing that raw chain-of-thought back in as plaintext, not just a summary. `encrypted_content` on `ReasoningItem` is always `None` here, so there is no encrypted-blob alternative to point callers at.

Two things follow from that: (1) a real per-turn token/context cost, since raw reasoning is typically far longer than a `reasoning.summary` would have been, and (2) a mild content-exposure consideration for multi-turn conversations, since the model's raw reasoning for turn N becomes part of the literal prompt text for turn N+1 rather than staying server-side. Neither is new to this PR's core behavior change (any caller already got the raw reasoning back once per turn when `reasoning.summary` was requested) — this PR just removes the last case where that could silently not happen, so it widens how often the cost applies rather than introducing it.

title: SITA Routing Policy and Score Shaping for Agentic Serving
body:
# SITA Routing Policy and Score Shaping This document describes two opt-in extensions to the KV router's default worker selector: 1. **SITA (Size-Interval Task Assignment)** — partitions the worker pool into contiguous bands and confines each request to the band matching its estimated work size, so long prefills stop queueing in front of short ones. 2. **Score shaping** — a set of `score_*` knobs that reshape the overlap credit and load term of the default worker logit, trading cache locality against load balance without replacing the stock cost function. Both features are **disabled by default**. With `sita_enabled: false` and `score_enabled: false`, worker selection is **byte-identical** to stock behavior — including tie-breaks and temperature sampling — which makes clean A/B comparisons possible. Neither feature's knobs appear in the serialized model deployment card unless set to non-default values, so older frontends can still read it. --- ## 1. SITA: Size-Interval Task Assignment ### Why the stock router is not enough The stock selector scores every worker with one cost function (`DefaultWorkerScorer::worker_logit`): ``` logit = prefill_load_scale × max(raw_prefill_blocks − overlap_credit, 0) # prefill backlog + decode_cost_blocks # decode backlog + decode_active_request_weight × active_requests # concurrency ``` and routes each request to the cheapest worker (or samples by temperature). The overlap credit is what makes it *KV-aware*: it prefers session affinity, pulling each request back to the worker that already holds its session's or template's KV blocks. That preference is exactly right for cache hit rate — and it is the failure mode on mixed-size traffic: **Affinity outranks waiting time.** A session-affine short request is pulled back to "its" worker even when that worker is mid-way through someone else's 16K-token prefill; the saved prefill (a few hundred tokens) is dwarfed by the seconds it now waits in line. The cost function cannot see this, because the load term counts backlog *blocks*, not *delay*: one 16K prefill and sixteen queued 1K prefills score identically, yet the short request waits the whole 16K service time behind the former and almost nothing behind the latter. With heavy-tailed ISL distributions this mispricing is constant, and every mitigation inside the formula (`overlap_score_credit_decay`, load weights) only re-tunes the exchange rate between affinity and load — it cannot express "this worker is fine for long jobs but poison for short ones." **And routing cannot fix it after the fact.** The router decides only *where* a request goes, never *when* the work already on a worker runs. Once a long prefill is committed, every short request whose affinity points there inherits the head-of-line blocking. The only routing-level fix is to keep short requests and long prefills out of the same queue in the first place — a partition, not a weight. SITA is that partition — the classical size-interval task assignment result: under heavy-tailed job sizes, segregating jobs by size beats any load-based dispatch, because it removes the size variance from each queue. Short requests only ever queue behind other short requests, so their TTFT stays low regardless of what the long tail is doing; long requests share the remaining workers, where queueing behind a peer costs proportionally less of their own service time. And SITA does not sacrifice affinity to get this — it *restructures* it: same-sized requests keep landing on the same few workers, so their shared prefixes (sessions, prompt templates, corpus chunks) concentrate there by construction, without the overlap credit having to win a bidding war against the load term. ### Mechanism When `sita_enabled` is true, the default worker selector: 1. **Sorts eligible workers by worker id** and partitions them into 2 or 3 contiguous bands. Band 0 (the short band) receives `ceil(sita_small_band_share × N)` workers (clamped to `[1, N−1]`); the remaining workers are split evenly across the longer bands, with the largest band always keeping at least one worker to itself. Every band is non-empty. 2. **Estimates the request's size** in tokens: ``` size = effective_prefill_tokens + sita_osl_weight × expected_output_tokens ``` `effective_prefill_tokens` is the prompt length minus the best cached overlap any eligible worker offers — a request whose prefix is already resident somewhere only counts the prefill it actually has to do. Requests without an output estimate contribute prefill only. 3. **Maps the size to a band**: band 0 if `size ≤ sita_boundary_1`, band 1 if `size ≤ sita_boundary_2`, band 2 otherwise. Setting `sita_boundary_2: 0` collapses the policy to a two-band split at `sita_boundary_1`. 4. **Confines scoring to that band**: the stock cost function then runs unchanged over only the band's workers, so temperature sampling, overlap credits, and load terms all behave as usual within the band. With the default knobs on an 8-worker pool (`sita_small_band_share: 0.5`): ``` worker id: 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 ┌─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┐ │ band 0 │ band 1 │ band 2 │ │ "short" │ "medium" │ "long" │ └───────────────────────┴───────────┴───────────┘ size ≤ 1024 ───────────►│ │ │ 1024 < size ≤ 8192 ─────────────────────►│ │ size > 8192 ────────────────────────────────────────►│ ``` SITA never changes routing when the pool has fewer than 2 eligible workers or when the request is pinned to a specific worker. ### Routing decision flow ```mermaid flowchart TD A{SITA on, ≥2 workers,
not pinned?} -- no --> S[Stock selection
over all workers] A -- yes --> B["size = effective_prefill + osl_weight × output
→ band via boundary_1 / boundary_2"] B --> C["Relief valves may widen the band:
• spill up if occupancy > threshold (top band: down to band 1)
• borrow band 0 while it is idle
• uncached long request → whole non-short pool"] C --> D[Stock cost function ranks
workers within the slice] ``` ### Relief valves Strict confinement alone wrecks tail latency, so three asymmetric escape hatches apply. All three are governed by `sita_spill_threshold`; at `1.0` they are all disabled and confinement is absolute. Occupancy is measured **relatively**: a band's score is the ratio of its mean per-worker queued work (queued prefill tokens plus resident decode blocks in token units) to the sum of its own mean and the rest of the pool's mean. An evenly loaded pool scores 0.5; the score rises toward 1.0 as the band gets busier than everyone else. This is what makes the `[0.5, 1.0]` threshold range meaningful — an absolute KV-capacity fraction would be a few percent under any realistic load and no threshold would ever trip. **Upward spill.** When a band's occupancy exceeds `sita_spill_threshold` and the band above it is genuinely quieter, the request may widen into that neighbor. Spilling *up* costs roughly the request's own service time; spilling a long request *down* would park a huge prefill in front of the short queue — the exact head-of-line blocking SITA exists to prevent — so band 0 is never a spill target on this path. **Top-band relief.** The largest band has no band above it. Without a relief valve it becomes a saturation sink — it receives spill from below and can never shed it, and the queue on its few workers blows up p99 end-to-end latency even as the mean improves. A saturated top band may therefore widen *down* into band 1 (medium requests), but still never into band 0. **Borrowing an idle short band.** Reserving workers for short requests is only free while short requests are actually using them. A statically fenced-off band 0 starves the long bands of KV capacity. So a saturated long band may borrow band 0's workers — but only while band 0's occupancy is below `1 − sita_spill_threshold`, i.e. measurably idle. The one threshold sets both directions of the dial: a high value means both a reluctance to spill and a strict definition of idle. Spill direction summary: ``` spill up (occupancy > t, neighbor quieter) band 0 ─────────► band 1 ─────────► band 2 ▲ ▲ │ │ borrow only └─────────────────┘ │ while band 0 top-band relief: │ occupancy widen down into band 1, │ < 1 − t never into band 0 └────────────────────┘ ``` ### Uncached long requests Band confinement pays for itself through cache affinity — but a request that matched **nothing** in any worker's cache has no affinity to preserve; it will prefill from scratch wherever it lands. Confining it buys nothing and costs plenty: long requests carry the largest resident KV and the longest decodes, so pinning them to a slice of the pool multiplies decode-batch contention exactly where inter-token latency already sets the end-to-end tail. A zero-overlap request in band 1 or 2 therefore always gets the **whole non-short pool**, and may additionally reach band 0 under a relaxed idleness bar of `2 × (1 − sita_spill_threshold)` — an uncached request is the cheapest possible borrower, since lending it a band-0 worker costs the short band only the load it brings, never a lost cache hit. Band 0 requests are never widened: a zero-overlap short request must not escape into the long workers. ### Configuration | Knob | Default | Range | Meaning | |---|---|---|---| | `sita_enabled` | `false` | — | Master switch. Off = stock routing, bit for bit. | | `sita_boundary_1` | `1024` | `> 0` | Upper size bound (tokens) of band 0. | | `sita_boundary_2` | `8192` | `0` or `> boundary_1` | Upper size bound of band 1. `0` selects a two-band split. | | `sita_osl_weight` | `0.0` | `≥ 0`, finite | Weight on expected output tokens in the size estimate. | | `sita_small_band_share` | `0.5` | `(0, 1)` exclusive | Fraction of the pool assigned to band 0. | | `sita_spill_threshold` | `0.85` | `[0.5, 1.0]` | Relative occupancy above which spill/borrow activates. `1.0` disables all relief valves. | Example: ```yaml kv_router_config: sita_enabled: true sita_boundary_1: 1024 sita_boundary_2: 8192 sita_small_band_share: 0.5 sita_spill_threshold: 0.85 sita_osl_weight: 0.0 ``` ### Choosing the hyperparameters **`sita_boundary_1` / `sita_boundary_2` — set from the *effective* ISL distribution, at its knees.** The band mapper sees the size *after* subtracting the best cached overlap any worker offers, so measure the distribution of `isl − cached_prefix` (or log `SITA band restricted routing` at debug level and histogram the reported `size`), not raw prompt length — a 2K-token request with a 1.8K cached template is a band-0 request. Put `boundary_1` just above the bulk of interactive traffic (the default 1024 suits chat-style prompts; raise it if your templates alone exceed 1K) and `boundary_2` below the long-context tail (RAG contexts, document dumps). If the workload is bimodal rather than trimodal, set `boundary_2: 0` and run two bands — a middle band with no traffic just fragments the pool. Boundaries are inclusive (`size ≤ boundary` stays in the lower band) and `boundary_2` must be 0 or strictly greater than `boundary_1`; the config loader rejects anything else. **`sita_small_band_share` — match the *work* share, not the request share.** Band 0 gets `ceil(share × N)` workers. Size it to the fraction of total token-work (prefill + decode) the short class carries, not the fraction of request count: short requests are usually 80–90% of requests but a much smaller share of tokens, so shares of 0.25–0.5 are typical. Too large starves the long bands of KV capacity (watch long-band occupancy pinning above the spill threshold and end-to-end p99 rising); too small makes band 0 itself spill (watch short-request TTFT and band-0 occupancy). On small pools remember the granularity: with `N = 8`, share 0.5 gives a 4/2/2 split and the minimum meaningful step is 1/N. The value must be strictly inside `(0, 1)`. **`sita_spill_threshold` — one dial, three valves; reason in relative-occupancy units.** Occupancy here is `band_mean / (band_mean + rest_of_pool_mean)`, so 0.5 means "as busy as everyone else." A threshold `t` simultaneously sets: spill out when a band's occupancy exceeds `t`; lend band 0 to a saturated long band when band 0's occupancy is below `1 − t`; and let an *uncached* long request borrow band 0 below `2 × (1 − t)`. At the default 0.85 that means: spill only when a band carries ~5.7× the per-worker load of the rest of the pool, lend band 0 when it carries under ~1/5.7 of the rest, and let uncached requests in below 0.30. Lower values (toward 0.5) favor utilization and tail latency at the cost of band isolation; `1.0` gives perfectly clean isolation for measurement runs but risks tail blow-up under skewed load because every relief valve is welded shut. Start at 0.85; move toward 0.7 if long-band p99 is the problem, toward 0.95 if short-request TTFT regresses under bursts. **`sita_osl_weight` — enable only when output length is predictable and dominant.** The default 0.0 classifies by prefill work alone, which is the right choice when `expected_output_tokens` is absent or unreliable (requests without an estimate contribute prefill only, so a nonzero weight would classify them inconsistently with their peers). Raise it when output, not prompt, dominates service time — reasoning or agentic workloads with short prompts and multi-thousand-token completions. At `1.0` an expected 2K-token completion counts the same as 2K prompt tokens; since decode tokens cost more wall-clock than prefill tokens, values ≥ 1.0 are defensible when the estimates are trustworthy. Must be finite and ≥ 0. **Validation and safety rails.** All ranges above are enforced at config load, on both the typed and JSON paths. The band partition guarantees every band is non-empty, band 0 is never widened, and pinned requests bypass SITA entirely — so no legal knob combination can strand a request with zero candidate workers. --- ## 2. Score shaping ### Why the stock logit's linearity fails The stock logit (above) is linear in both of its competitive terms, and each linearity has a failure mode: - **The overlap credit is linear in absolute overlap**, so a thin 5% prefix match pulls a request toward a worker at the same per-block rate as a 95% match. Thin matches are rarely worth the pull — the request still pays nearly its full prefill, but it forgoes a less-loaded worker to get there. The existing `overlap_score_credit_decay` shrinks credit on *backlogged* workers, but it cannot distinguish a thin match from a deep one on an idle worker. - **The load term is linear**, so a worker already twice as busy as the pool average is only charged twice as much. Cache affinity systematically creates such hot spots (that is its job), and a linear charge lets them keep winning ties on deep prefix hits well past the point where their decode batch is saturated and inter-token latency degrades for everyone resident there. Score shaping bends both curves without replacing the formula, so the stock behavior remains the exactly-recoverable neutral point. ### Mechanism When `score_enabled` is true, two terms are reshaped. The **neutral knob set** (all weights and gammas `1.0`, `score_min_overlap_frac` `0.0`) reproduces the stock logit *exactly* — the shaping is multiplicative around 1.0 and the neutral case preserves the original floating-point summation order, so results are bit-identical rather than merely close. ``` stock: credit linear in overlap shaped: cutoff + bent curve credit ▲ credit ▲ │ / │ . - ˙ γ = 0.5 │ / │ . ˙ / │ / │ ˙ / γ = 1 │ / │ ˙ / _/ │ / │ ˙ / _/ γ = 2 │/ │ 0 ────┐ / _/ └──────────────────► overlap_frac └────────┴──────────► overlap_frac 0 1 0 │ 1 min_overlap_frac (credit = 0 below cutoff) ``` **Overlap credit.** Let `overlap_frac` be the fraction of the request's blocks the worker already holds. The shaped credit is: ``` credit = 0 if overlap_frac < score_min_overlap_frac credit = score_overlap_weight × overlap_frac^(score_overlap_gamma − 1) × stock_credit otherwise ``` The `gamma − 1` exponent on the fraction, applied multiplicatively to the stock credit, is algebraically `overlap_frac^gamma × request_blocks` — it bends the response curve while keeping the host, disk, and shared cache tiers on the same curve. Gamma above 1.0 concentrates credit on near-full prefix hits; below 1.0 spreads it toward partial hits. Zero-overlap workers earn nothing under any gamma. **Load term.** The decode-side backlog is charged convexly relative to the mean load across eligible workers: ``` load_cost = score_load_weight × (load_term / mean_pool_load)^(score_load_gamma − 1) × load_term ``` With `score_load_gamma > 1.0`, a worker hotter than the pool average pays superlinearly, which actively pushes work off hot spots; a worker at the mean pays exactly its linear share (the ratio is 1.0, so the shape factor vanishes). ### Configuration | Knob | Default | Range | Meaning | |---|---|---|---| | `score_enabled` | `false` | — | Master switch. Off = stock logit, bit for bit, regardless of other knobs. | | `score_overlap_weight` | `1.0` | `[0.25, 4.0]` | Multiplier on the shaped overlap credit. `> 1` chases cache locality harder; `< 1` prefers load balance. | | `score_overlap_gamma` | `1.0` | `[0.5, 2.0]` | Exponent on the overlap fraction. `> 1` favors near-full hits; `< 1` favors partial hits. | | `score_load_weight` | `1.0` | `[0.25, 4.0]` | Multiplier on the decode-side load term. | | `score_load_gamma` | `1.0` | `[1.0, 2.0]` | Convexity of the load term vs. the pool mean. `> 1` charges hot spots superlinearly. | | `score_min_overlap_frac` | `0.0` | `[0.0, 0.5]` | Minimum overlap fraction before any credit is granted; suppresses thin prefix matches. | Example: ```yaml kv_router_config: score_enabled: true score_overlap_weight: 1.5 score_overlap_gamma: 1.25 score_load_gamma: 1.4 score_min_overlap_frac: 0.1 ``` ### Choosing the hyperparameters **Start from neutral and move one knob at a time.** Neutral (`1.0/1.0/1.0/1.0/0.0` with `score_enabled: true`) is bit-identical to stock, so every deviation is attributable. The validation ranges are deliberately tight — weights within `[0.25, 4.0]`, overlap gamma within `[0.5, 2.0]`, load gamma within `[1.0, 2.0]` (concavity is disallowed: charging hot workers *less* than linearly is never useful), cutoff within `[0.0, 0.5]` — so no legal value can invert the cost function's basic ordering. **`score_min_overlap_frac` — set from your cache-hit distribution.** Histogram `overlap_frac` (overlap blocks ÷ request blocks) from router debug logs. There is usually a bimodal shape: near-full template hits and a dust cloud of incidental short matches. Put the cutoff in the valley — commonly 0.1–0.2. The cap of 0.5 exists because suppressing majority-overlap hits is always a loss. **`score_overlap_gamma` — how much a partial hit is really worth.** If prefill cost is roughly linear in uncached tokens, the stock linear credit is correct and gamma stays 1.0. Raise it (1.25–1.5) when partial hits under-deliver in practice — e.g. the matched prefix is cold by arrival, or chunked prefill amortizes the saving — so only deep hits justify the locality pull. Lower it (0.75) when even partial template hits measurably cut TTFT and you want them chased. **`score_load_gamma` — the hot-spot corrector.** This is the knob to reach for when a few cache-hot workers show sustained above-mean decode load and degraded inter-token latency while their peers idle. 1.25–1.5 is a gentle corrector; 2.0 charges a 2×-mean worker 2× extra and behaves close to a soft cap. Note the reference point is the *mean over currently eligible workers*, recomputed per request — under SITA band confinement the mean is the band's mean, so the two features compose sensibly. **`score_overlap_weight` / `score_load_weight` — global tilt, last resort.** These scale whole terms rather than bending curves, so they blunt-force the locality-vs-balance trade-off: raise `score_overlap_weight` above 1.0 only if cache hit rate is the dominant cost (long shared prefixes, expensive prefill) and load is comfortably provisioned; raise `score_load_weight` when balance matters more than hit rate. Prefer the gammas and the cutoff first — they fix the *shape* problems; the weights just re-fight the stock trade-off at a different exchange rate. --- ## Interaction and guarantees - SITA and score shaping are **independent**: SITA restricts *which* workers are candidates; score shaping changes *how* candidates are ranked. Either can be enabled alone, or both together (SITA narrows the pool, then the shaped logit ranks within it — and the shaped load term's pool mean is then the band's mean). - **Off means off.** Each feature's non-default knobs are inert while its `*_enabled` flag is false; disabled selection is identical to stock across tie-breaks and temperature sampling (covered by seeded A/B tests). - **Pinned workers always win**, regardless of band. - **Validation is strict**: out-of-range knobs are rejected at config load, both from the typed and the JSON paths (e.g. `sita_boundary_2` must be `0` or strictly greater than `sita_boundary_1`; `sita_small_band_share` is exclusive on both ends). - **Serialization is backward-compatible**: default values are skipped when serializing, and absent fields deserialize to defaults. --- ## Results Measured on Qwen3-32B over 8× Blackwell 183 GiB (one worker per GPU), Dynamo KV router built from source with sglang 0.5.18, driven by aiperf open-loop replay: a heavy-tailed synthetic stress trace (n=3 runs) and a held-out real Claude Code trace (n=2 runs). Five arms were compared against the stock KV router: banding alone, fixed load convexity at γ=2.0 and γ=1.5, adaptive γ, and the composition of bands + convexity (SITA + score shaping). Only the composition survives replication — banding alone is tail-toxic, γ=1.5 alone looked strong at n=2 but its whiskers cross zero at n=3, and adaptive γ is safe but diluted. The composition's win splits cleanly by mechanism: **bands give the median** — short requests get a clean lane, cutting heavy-trace p50 E2E by 13.2% and mean TTFT by 18.3% — while **convexity gives the tail**, leveling the long lane for a 58.2% reduction in heavy-trace p99 TTFT (worst individual run still −38%). The wins transfer to the held-out real traffic: on the Claude Code trace, p99 TTFT improves 15.7%, p50 E2E 8.6%, and mean and p99 E2E 5.8% each. Every latency metric beat stock in every individual run on both traces, and the throughput cost is not measurable (tok/s −0.4% on the stress trace, −0.1% on Claude Code). ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **New Features** * Added optional request-size-aware routing that groups workers into configurable size bands, helping direct requests to suitable workers while allowing controlled spillover when bands are busy. * Added optional score shaping to adjust routing based on request overlap and worker load. * Added configuration options for both features, with defaults that preserve existing routing behavior. Invalid setting values are rejected.

title: docs(operator): clarify worker ReadinessProbe gates external KubeDiscoveryClient routing
body: ## Overview One-line-scope change: **comment-only** edit in `deploy/operator/internal/dynamo/component_worker.go` (no code change, no test change). Rewords a pre-existing comment block that was factually correct for Dynamo's internal KvStore transport but misled multiple downstream deployments when the Frontend's `KubeDiscoveryClient` path is in play. ## Problem The pre-existing comment (lines 54–56 in `main` at the time of this patch) reads: ```go // ReadinessProbe in Dynamo worker context doesn't determine that the worker is ready to receive traffic // Since worker registration is done through external KvStore and Transport does not use Kubernetes Service // Still important for external depencies that rely on Pod Readiness ``` This is half-true. It's accurate for the NATS/etcd KvStore transport (Dynamo's internal routing). It's **not** accurate for any deployment where Frontend uses the k8s-native discovery path — which is the default when the operator provisions a `Service` for worker pods. The runtime's `KubeDiscoveryClient` at [`lib/runtime/src/discovery/kube/daemon.rs:246`](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/main/lib/runtime/src/discovery/kube/daemon.rs) explicitly filters EndpointSlices by `endpoint.conditions.ready == true` before correlating them with `DynamoWorkerMetadata` CRs. Workers whose Pod Ready stays `False` during model load (large LLM weight load, cudagraph capture, NIXL handshake) are filtered out of the Frontend's instance map, even though the worker has registered its CR and is serving traffic over the internal KvStore transport. The net effect: Frontend `/v1/models` returns `{"data":[]}` and `/v1/completions` returns HTTP 404 for up to 5+ minutes, with no obvious diagnostic unless you read both the Rust daemon and the Go operator code side by side. ## Fix Replace the 3-line comment with an 11-line block that: 1. States explicitly that `ReadinessProbe` **does** gate external Kubernetes Service / EndpointSlice routing 2. Names the runtime file + line (`lib/runtime/src/discovery/kube/daemon.rs:246`) where that filtering happens 3. Clarifies that the prior wording was only correct for the internal KvStore transport 4. Cross-links the reproducing case ([ai-dynamo/dynamo#9200](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/9200)) No function, probe config, or container mutation is touched. Pure doc change. ## Why this is worth merging - **Zero risk.** Compile is unaffected; probe behavior is unchanged. - **Real operational value.** At least one deployment ([aws-samples/awsome-inference#72](https://github.com/aws-samples/awsome-inference/pull/72)) traced a 6-revision debugging cycle to the ambiguity in this exact comment. - **Preserves the original author's intent** — they were correct about the KvStore case. The fix just adds the Service-routing case on equal footing. ## Testing - [x] Comment-only; existing unit tests cover `container.ReadinessProbe` assertions unchanged - [x] Local `git diff --stat` confirms only `component_worker.go` touched - [ ] No functional regression expected (requires CI confirm) ## Linked - Fixes half of [#9200](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/9200) (documentation side; the operational side, whether the probe's default `failureThreshold: 3` is too tight for typical model-load times, is a potential follow-up PR) ## Downstream context This contribution originated from the [aws-samples/awsome-inference#72](https://github.com/aws-samples/awsome-inference/pull/72) PR which bundles Dynamo + AWS EFA RDMA + 1.0.1 → 1.1.0 bump. Happy to move the PR to a nvidia.com-hosted fork if that's the preferred contribution flow for the Dynamo repo; please let me know. --- ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Documentation** * Updated internal documentation for container configuration readiness probe details. --- **Note:** This release contains internal documentation improvements with no user-facing changes or functional updates.

title: fix(recipes): K-EXAONE 2.0 review follow-ups — Fern-only docs, IB component, image and resource hygiene
body:
Follow-up to the best-practices review on #14822, plus the two review comments from the launch
thread. Everything here is verified on 8x B200 — see Validation.

## Related Issues

Relates to #14822

## Fixed

**Documentation is now Fern-only** (review 23, 25)
- `recipes/k-exaone-2.0/README.md` collapsed 295 -> 20 lines: a pointer to the rendered page plus
  the variant table. The three notes that existed only in the README — the supported-features
  table, KV-aware routing scale-out behaviour, and the absence of a cache-clearing endpoint —
  were migrated into the Fern page so nothing was lost.
- Manifest headers and in-body comments trimmed to the correctness constraints a reader cannot
  infer from the flag name. The internal tuning narrative (block-size and TP sweeps, prefix-reuse
  analysis) is gone.

**InfiniBand config moved out of the base** (review 3)
- `rdma/shared_ib`, `UCX_TLS` and `NCCL_IB_DISABLE` now live in
  `kustomize/components/ib`; the base carries no fabric configuration at all. This is cluster
  networking, not model configuration.
- The rendered manifest is renamed `deploy-generic.yaml` -> **`deploy-ib.yaml`**, so it is clear
  the fabric settings are pre-injected and a reader does not layer their own on top. It also
  stops colliding with the meaning `deploy-generic.yaml` already carries elsewhere in this repo,
  where it is the render with *no* provider networking.
- No generic render is shipped for the disaggregated target: without an RDMA resource that
  configuration is untested here, and an unvalidated manifest is worse than none.

**Images pinned by digest** (review 15)
- Both images pinned to their multi-arch **index** digest, tag retained for readability. A
  `-post.N` tag is mutable and a recipe is a reproduction claim.

**Resource requests declared** (review 20, 21, 22)
- Workers: `cpu: 16`, `ephemeral-storage: 64Gi`.
- Frontend: `cpu: 8`, `memory: 16Gi`, `ephemeral-storage: 16Gi` — it previously had none, and a
  frontend pulling an image with no ephemeral-storage request is how a CPU node ran out of disk
  during this recipe's bring-up.
- `sharedMemorySize` 40Gi -> 64Gi, and the duplicate `dshm` `emptyDir` removed (the operator
  already provides `/dev/shm`; verified as a 64G tmpfs in the running container).
- The `480Gi` memory limit dropped, leaving requests only. GPU and `rdma/shared_ib` stay in
  `limits`, where extended resources are required.

**Security context** (review 4, 5)
- `runAsGroup: 0` alongside `runAsUser: 0` on all three workers.
- `SYS_PTRACE` added to the aggregated worker. The two variants disagreed — disagg had all three
  capabilities, agg had `[IPC_LOCK, SYS_RESOURCE]` — so this was a slip, not a choice.

**`imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent`** on every container (review 16).

**Benchmark doc correction** — the note claimed the shipped `perf.yaml` sends a fresh
`cache_salt` per run. It does not; its only `--extra-inputs` value is `ignore_eos:true`, so
successive concurrency points inherited the previous point's prefix cache. Now states what the
job actually does and keeps the restart requirement, matching `perf/README.md`.

## Deliberately not changed

- **`runtimeVersionOverride` is kept** (review 18). The operator cannot parse a version out of a
  digest-pinned reference, and the merged `ax-k2` recipe ships the same tag shape and keeps the
  override. Dropping it breaks the deployment.
- **The frontend stays on `dynamo-frontend:1.4.1`** rather than the worker image (review 17). It
  is CPU-only and loads no weights; the model-specific runtime is far larger, and pulling it onto
  a CPU frontend node previously exhausted ephemeral storage.
- **Frontend requests are `cpu 8 / 16Gi`, not the reviewed `16 / 128Gi`.** Two conventions exist
  in this repo — `4-8 CPU / 16Gi` (nemotron-3-ultra, gpt-oss-120b) and `16 / 128Gi`
  (solar-open2-250b). The latter assumes fat CPU nodes: on a cluster whose CPU nodes are 32 core
  / 63Gi it is unschedulable, and because the operator gang-schedules, the frontend alone holds
  the workers `Pending` too. Caught in validation.

## Deferred

The portable-contract items (`shared-model-cache` naming and mount path, frontend cache mount,
exec-form `command`, DGD naming convention) change mount paths and service names, so each needs
its own validation run. They are deliberately left for a separate PR so this one stays reviewable
and does not invalidate the validation already done on the merged recipe.

## Validation

Both variants deployed from the rendered manifests on 8x B200 and smoke-tested after every
behavioural change:

- Coherence on three prompt shapes including Korean; tool calling returns `finish_reason:
  tool_calls`; `FLASHINFER_CUTLASS` confirmed selected in the worker log.
- Disaggregated KV transfer over IB RDMA confirmed by `vllm:nixl_xfer_time_seconds` — sub-millisecond
  to low-millisecond means, cross-node.
- All environment variables read back from the **running container**, confirming the Kustomize
  component merges into `spec.env` rather than replacing it.
- Digest-pinned images, resource requests and the 64G `/dev/shm` all verified on running pods.

Depends on #15064 for the `spec.env` merge key, which is merged.

title: feat(sidecar): add multimodal-aware vLLM KV routing
body:
#### Summary

The KV router matches cached blocks by hashing the token ids in each KV event. For an image, the frontend (built with `mm-routing`) replaces each image placeholder run with a pad value derived from the image hash. The worker's KV event publisher must apply the same rewrite, and for that it needs the model's image placeholder token. The vLLM sidecar publisher always sent `image_token_id: None`, so image blocks never matched and a repeated image request reused only its text prefix.

This PR resolves the image placeholder token in the vLLM sidecar and passes it to the KV event publisher.

Repro (frontend wheel built with `--features mm-routing`):

```bash
vllm-rs serve Qwen/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct --grpc-port 50051 --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image":1}' \
  -- --kv-events-config '{"publisher":"zmq","topic":"kv-events","endpoint":"tcp://*:5557","enable_kv_cache_events":true}'
dynamo-vllm-sidecar --grpc-endpoint 127.0.0.1:50051
DYN_LOG=info,dynamo_llm::kv_router=debug python -m dynamo.frontend --router-mode kv --kv-cache-block-size 16
# Send the same text + image chat request twice and read the "[ROUTING] ... blocks overlap" line.
```

Second request with the same image:

```text
before: [ROUTING] Best: worker_... dp_rank=0 with 8/74 blocks overlap
after:  [ROUTING] Best: worker_... dp_rank=0 with 73/74 blocks overlap
```

#### Details

- **The sidecar resolves the token.** The sidecar turns vLLM's KV events into router hashes, and vLLM's gRPC `ModelInfo` does not report the placeholder token. The sidecar calls the resolver that the frontend uses, so both sides get the same token.
- **Resolve once, fall back on failure.** The token is fixed for a model, so the sidecar resolves it once at start. Exact routing is an optimization, so a slow or missing model hub must not block startup: the fetch stops at the startup deadline, and image requests keep text-prefix routing.
- **A fallback cannot misroute.** The router accepts only a frontend-issued image hash in a KV event. A mismatch between the two sides loses reuse but never matches a different image.
- **`supports_multimodal` is part of the model identity.** The token comes from the model seen at start, so startup fails if its multimodal support differs from the model registered at bootstrap.
- **`mm-routing` is a sidecar feature, on by default.** The Python bindings compile the sidecar in. They turn the feature off and forward their own opt-in `mm-routing`, so the default wheel stays lean.

#### Validation

One frontend with the KV router in front of two vLLM sidecar workers, serving `Qwen/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct`. Every request has the same text and one image, so only the image can steer placement. Images A and B go out first at the same time, so load puts them on different workers. Then A and B alternate four times each, then a new image C and one repeat. Each run starts with cold engines.

| | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A/B repeats routed to the worker that holds the image | 4 of 8 | 8 of 8 |
| Router overlap on A/B repeats | 8/74 (text only) | 73/74 |
| New image C, first request / repeat | 8/74, 8/74 | 8/74, 73/74 (same worker) |
| vLLM prefix-cache hits, both engines | 61% (8,560 of 14,040 tokens) | 76% (10,640 of 14,040 tokens) |

On main both workers hold only the shared text, so the router sees a tie and half the repeats land on the worker without the image.

#### Related Issues

- [x] Confirmed: no related issue

title: feat: Log frontend NUMA CPU affinity
body:
## Overview:

Warn when the frontend's effective CPU affinity spans multiple NUMA nodes before the Tokio runtime is created.

## Details:

No API from this PR or local dependency override is used. The existing full Dynamo adapter already provided native KV selection; the new AISimulate-side adapter adds conversation configuration and lifecycle/cache-event wiring.

The consumer is installed and exercised end to end. Matching release wheels and an independent clean-source container at AISimulate runtime `e9d5d279` each passed **60 native-policy/CLI plus 28 admission tests**, with actual worker/DP bindings and physical cache reuse. The package remains source-built, not index-published. See [AISimulate #306](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/aisimulate/pull/306) for exact artifact provenance, final review status and remaining human merge gates.

**The requested feature does not justify merging this PR as a prerequisite.** The API conveniences below may be evaluated independently by Dynamo maintainers. Current head `62482597` has passing Pre Merge and Full PR CI, remains OPEN / REVIEW_REQUIRED, and has not been merged. CODEOWNER approval and review resolution remain required if this separate scope is pursued.

## Summary

Allow an external simulation host to compose Dynamo's native KV worker selection with session or sibling-group affinity. The host advances virtual time and commits a worker/DP binding only after dispatch is accepted.

- Add a public eligibility helper shared with the live scheduler. An external caller of the existing selector can now apply the same eligible affinity constraint as the production queue, including worker availability, allowlists and DP rank validation. Affinity eligibility uses the final availability set, independent of builder order, and reactivates when availability is restored. Custom policies retain advisory affinity semantics.
- Add a manual-clock constructor to the native `SessionAffinity` table, preserving native initialization, wait, commit, invalidation, lease and idle-expiry behavior. Active leases survive virtual TTL; release starts idle expiry at virtual time. Manual construction and advancement reject values whose TTL deadline would overflow, before mutating bindings or time. The normal runtime-clock constructor is unchanged.
- Publish the sibling-group key helper, add external-crate contract tests, and document the public embedding contract and installation/build requirements.
- Fix the benchmark `OnceLock<Instant>` inference error that blocked root Rust tests and Clippy.

This PR targets `main` directly. Rust, Python, containers and standalone lockfiles all retain published AISimulate **0.12.0**, with the existing strict consistency checks. It has no dependency on [AISimulate #306](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/aisimulate/pull/306) or the unmerged Dynamo #14521. The public `dynamo-kv-router` crate has no AISimulate dependency.

## Validation

- Public native API contracts: 11 passed. KV-router library: 1274 passed, 2 existing ignored. The added real-selector regression reproduces `NoEndpoints` before the availability-order fix and passes afterward; one redundant private lifecycle test was removed while retaining the public lifecycle contract. Executable Rust examples: 2 passed.
- An external consumer outside every workspace successfully runs the documented lifecycle with `cargo run --locked`, using the published immutable candidate Git revision `62482597db839fcd657f2e39596c4071572a3408`. The same external Git-linked project passes all 11 public API tests, including availability-order, explicit-pin consistency and manual-clock overflow coverage, with Rust/Cargo 1.96.1. Its lockfile and dependency tree contain Dynamo routing/hashing/tokens/truthy at that revision, with no AISimulate, Dynamo runtime, LLM or Mocker dependency and no path/patch override. This qualifies the current native candidate installation and public contracts; it does not establish a merged release or AISimulate CLI availability.
- Rebuilt real Python native bindings against published AISimulate 0.12.0: all 26 previously failing runtime/planner/profiler/router functional cases plus 7 strict dependency checks pass together, 33/33 with no skips. Mocker library: 217/217 passed.
- Root all-target Clippy and router all-target Clippy pass with warnings denied. The exact failed `dc_ckf_relay` benchmark Clippy and test compilation pass. Four Cargo workspaces pass locked metadata checks; all three AISimulate lock entries resolve the same crates.io 0.12.0 release.
- Rust formatting, relevant pre-commit hooks, strict ownership coverage and generated ownership-file checks pass. Docs lint and Fern configuration checks pass. Fern broken-link checking reports an existing link in the unchanged `deepseek-v4-pro-0813.mdx` recipe; it does not report a new-page failure (the tool exits 0 despite that finding).
- Current head `62482597db839fcd657f2e39596c4071572a3408` fixes the availability-order, redundant-test/comment and manual-clock overflow findings. Its [Pre Merge](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/actions/runs/35676622259) is fully successful, including all 11 public API contracts, root Rust tests/doc tests, feature-gated benchmark compilation and all Clippy jobs. All six formerly failing container CPU jobs now pass: Planner amd64/arm64, Runtime parallel amd64/arm64, and Runtime sequential amd64/arm64. Strict dependency consistency checks pass with published AISimulate 0.12.0. The [Full PR](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/actions/runs/35676625791) has now passed, including the previously pending backend jobs. The preceding `e1fb03fa` and `c656bc34` CI results are historical. Required CI, CODEOWNERS review and resolved review threads remain separate merge gates. Review note: the suggestion to bypass eligible affinity whenever an explicit pin exists was not adopted. The [pre-PR main queue](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/f3c7c225aa3d1a117b7c1bddefcd98b1772db558/lib/kv-router/src/scheduling/queue.rs#L1626-L1633) already applies both constraints, and SessionAffinity validates that explicit worker/DP targets agree with an existing binding. title: fix(trtllm): normalize multimodal KV events
body:
## Summary

- normalize TensorRT-LLM V2 multimodal KV events into the same routing-token representation used by requests
- consume the frontend routing identity from the additive `mm_keys[].uuid` field introduced by NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM#19529 while retaining `mm_keys[].hash` as the content digest
- fail closed on missing or malformed block-local multimodal metadata, including invalid token-ID types, while allowing later events to continue
- use TensorRT-LLM's `resolve_vocab_size()` for the continuation-token offset
- pin the forward fixture to the exact TensorRT-LLM #19529 serializer contract and retain a separately labeled legacy fixture
- distinguish text-prefix-only router matches from full text-and-image matches in TensorRT-LLM end-to-end tests

## Validation

- latest commit-time pre-commit hooks passed
- latest focused TensorRT-LLM publisher, image-token-resolver, and cached-token payload tests — 86 passed
- TensorRT-LLM `resolve_vocab_size()` smoke check for Qwen3-VL — `151936`
- TensorRT-LLM V1 multimodal routing E2E — passed with a repeated-request router hit rate of `0.909`
- TensorRT-LLM V2 multimodal routing E2E against NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM#19529 — passed with the strict full-match threshold (`router_kv_hit_rate > 0.5`) before the review-only follow-up

The latest follow-up could not be rerun through the model E2E because the retained validation image's compiled Dynamo core predates the checked-out frontend API; both attempts stopped before server startup. The valid event output remains covered by the focused identity and publisher-path tests above.

## Notes

This PR depends on the exact NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM#19529 event contract pinned by the fixture at `687d95a29106e642d3f38b81ae193ac5d0aa6ee2`. Dynamo intentionally decodes that fixed serialized shape without compatibility branches for hypothetical future formats. No TensorRT-LLM changes are part of this follow-up.

The request and event paths use the same frontend identity: Dynamo forwards the 16-hex routing hash as `multi_modal_uuids`; TensorRT-LLM preserves it in `mm_keys[].uuid`; Dynamo converts that UUID to the canonical multimodal pad token. The content digest remains in `mm_keys[].hash` for block-local validation. Cross-block item consistency remains TensorRT-LLM's responsibility.

`gen_multimodal_cache_key_tokens()` is intentionally not used: it generates producer-side cache-key tokens from an unexpanded multimodal item, while Dynamo consumes already-expanded serialized event tokens and must recover their block positions.

title: fix(tests): pin SGLang router worker NCCL ports and gate on /health
body:
Source issue: [DYN-4249](https://linear.app/nvidia/issue/DYN-4249).

## Overview:

`tests/router/test_router_e2e_with_sglang.py::test_sglang_kv_router_basic` fails roughly once in three hundred runs with `AssertionError: Timeout waiting for workers. Found 1 instance(s), expected 2`. This removes the likely cause and makes that class of failure report itself instead of timing out silently.

## Details:

The test's workers let SGLang pick the `torch.distributed` rendezvous port. `get_free_port()` binds to port 0, reads the number and closes the socket, and the non-data-parallel path never re-checks it, so the port can be taken before `init_process_group` binds it and the losing worker blocks in rendezvous with no VRAM and no exit. That chain is inferred from the engine's port-selection source plus a CI trace showing the second worker at 0 GiB for the whole window; no run here reproduced a collision. `examples/backends/sglang/launch/disagg_same_gpu.sh` already names this race and prescribes `--nccl-port`, so each worker now takes a port from the shared `flock`-backed registry, as `tests/fault_tolerance/migration/test_sglang.py` does.

Each worker is also gated on its own system-port `/health`. Both check lists were empty, so the harness's per-worker health and liveness checks did nothing and a dead or hung worker stayed silent until the frontend poll gave up. Three limits worth knowing: the previously inert `timeout=120` is now the binding per-worker deadline (a healthy worker reaches ready in about 23 s today); a ready `/health` proves the `generate` endpoint registered, not that the engine can serve a request; and both workers write one log file, so the tail printed on failure is not reliably the failing worker's — the exit code and the preceding `Checking health for worker N` line identify it. `DYN_SYSTEM_USE_ENDPOINT_HEALTH_STATUS` stays unset deliberately: a non-empty value replaces the registered-payload mechanism with a deprecated one, and the gate works without it.

Draft #14182 targets the same failure; its readiness-gate idea is adopted here. The rest is not carried over: it conflicts with `main` after #14499, pairs its gate with that deprecated variable, leaves the rendezvous port unmanaged, and was never run on a GPU.

## Where should the reviewer start?

`SGLangProcess.__init__` in `tests/router/test_router_e2e_with_sglang.py`: the `_nccl_ports` allocation with its finalizer, and the `health_check_urls` entry.

## Validation

Lint and collection pass. On an A100 both workers take distinct allocated rendezvous ports, pass `/health`, and register on the frontend's first poll. With a deliberately broken second worker the current code fails after `195.85s` with the unattributed timeout above, and the gated code fails after `29.18s` naming worker 1 and its exit code. The test itself cannot pass on that card — `fused_topk_deepseek does not support compute capability 80` fails identically with and without the change — so the end-to-end pass, and any claim about the residual flake rate, belong to `sglang-runtime / Test cuda13.0, amd64`.

title: test(sglang): pin the rendezvous port in the tool-calling fixture
body:
Source issue: [DYN-4424](https://linear.app/nvidia/issue/DYN-4424).

## Summary

The SGLang tool-calling fixture launched its worker without `--nccl-port`, so SGLang picked the `torch.distributed` rendezvous port itself by binding port 0 and closing the socket, long before `init_process_group` binds it for real. Nothing holds the port in between, and the number comes from the kernel's ephemeral range, so another listener can take it and startup dies with an address-in-use error. This pins the port from the range the suite reserves, as `tests/fault_tolerance/migration/test_sglang.py` already does.

That removes a real startup race, but it is not a diagnosis of the reported flake: with the port deliberately occupied, startup fails with `exited with code -9`, not the `code 1` on the issue. The issue should stay open.

## Details:

- `tool_calling_services` allocates a fourth port from `DynamoPortRange.NCCL` and passes it to the worker as `--nccl-port`.
- `WorkerProcess.__init__` gains a keyword-only `nccl_port`.
- The NCCL reservation joins the existing tracked allocation list, so setup failures and teardown release it with the other ports. Main's separate port ranges, delayed frontend allocation, and `finally` cleanup are preserved.

No production code, timeout value, or assertion changed.

## Where should the reviewer start?

`tests/frontend/test_tool_calling_sglang.py`, and in it the teardown order in `tool_calling_services`: ports are released only after the straggler sweep.

## Validation

Remote CI on `57e16d8cb3fbbc34bc169d1ab8b432352858864a`: the [SGLang AMD64 test job](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/actions/runs/35761341978/job/106862068809) passed all 22 cases in `tests/frontend/test_tool_calling_sglang.py` (11 per topology: 16 protocol cases and 6 multi-turn cases). title: feat(frontend): support Kimi Code request fields on /v1/chat/completions
body:
## Summary

Kimi Code CLI (Moonshot, `@moonshot-ai/kimi-code`) sends request shapes the frontend rejected or silently dropped on `/v1/chat/completions`. The schema additions live in `dynamo-protocols` (ai-dynamo/frontend-crates#211); this PR consumes them and adds the Dynamo-side normalization. No new CLI flags — every change is additive and only takes effect when the request carries the field.

| Field | Sent by Kimi Code | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| `prompt_cache_key`, `safety_identifier` (OpenAI-standard) | every request | 400 `Unsupported parameter(s)` | typed request fields (frontend-crates#211); forwarded, not acted on — routing already keys on prompt prefix |
| `{"role":"system","tools":[…]}` with no `content` (K3 dynamic tool loading) | when dynamic tools on | deserialization error | accepted; `tools` reaches the chat template via the existing `serde_json::to_value(messages)` render path |
| `tools[].type: "builtin_function"` (`$web_search`) | not yet (documented) | rejected | accepted, rendered like a function; `$` prefix passes tool-name validation only for this type |
| assistant `partial: true` on the final message | not yet (documented) | silently dropped | `normalize_partial_final_message` → `continue_final_message = true`, `add_generation_prompt` defaults to `false`; an explicit `add_generation_prompt: true` still fails validation |
| `thinking.effort` (`low`/`high`/`max`) | yes | silently dropped — only `thinking.type` read | joins the `reasoning_effort` fallback chain (top-level `reasoning_effort` still wins) |
| `thinking.keep: "all"` | yes | silently dropped | → `chat_template_args.preserve_thinking = true` (the key the Kimi templates read) |
| `reasoning_effort` on K3 (Rust render path) | via the above | template reads `thinking_effort`, so effort never applied | mapped to `thinking_effort` when the `kimi_k3` tool parser is active (Rust counterpart of #13120) |

Struct literals of `ChatCompletionRequestSystemMessage` / `ChatCompletionRequestAssistantMessage` gain `tools: None` / `partial: None`.

**Blocked on release:** `Cargo.toml` temporarily points `dynamo-protocols` at the `kimi-code-compat` branch via `[patch.crates-io]` and bumps the pin to `=5.4.1`. Once frontend-crates#211 is released, drop the patch section and pin the released version.

Supersedes #14331 and #14332 (the latter carried an interim passthrough-list workaround in Dynamo; per team preference the protocol change goes in frontend-crates first).

## Validation

- `cargo check -p dynamo-llm --no-default-features --all-targets` clean
- `cargo test -p dynamo-llm --no-default-features --lib -- partial kimi_typed thinking validate_no_unsupported_fields kimi_k3 continue_final validate_tools` → 113 passed (10 new tests)

title: fix(sglang): propagate validation aborts as request errors
body:
## Summary

- Return SGLang validation aborts as request errors before placeholder tokens or a successful finish can be emitted.
- Preserve public validation errors through the native response iterator and optional Python SGLang frontend.
- Wrap the Python frontend's generic error responses as terminal error events. Preserve ordinary cancellation and shutdown behavior.

## Before / after behavior

For non-streaming requests:

| Request | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `"type":"invalid_type"` | HTTP 200 + `stop` + unrelated token | HTTP 400 + compiler message |
| `"pattern":"[unclosed["` | HTTP 200 + `stop` + unrelated token | HTTP 400 + compiler message |
| Valid schema | HTTP 200 with valid JSON | Unchanged |

If streaming headers have already been sent, HTTP remains 200; the validation failure is delivered as a terminal SSE error instead of a successful finish.

## Concern: no frontend schema precheck

- **No new semantic JSON Schema validation is added at frontend request admission.** Existing JSON parsing and basic checks remain unchanged.
- SGLang validates after backend dispatch. Dynamo propagates its rejection.
- The native iterator preserves explicitly public validation messages; other error classes retain their existing handling.

## Validation

- **Checks:** Applicable pre-commit hooks, Rust formatting, and whitespace checks passed.
- **Worker harness:** 45 source-level cases passed with mocked I/O and native exception stand-ins.
- **Frontend regression:** Seven source-level cases passed; all five error regressions failed against the previous code while both controls passed.
- **Native checks:** 39 Rust tests and 29 iterator scenarios passed in a compiled extracted-source harness. Eight before/after combinations through the native iterator, Python frontend, and Rust error mapping confirm both fixes are needed.

- **Limits:** Harnesses use extracted source. Full latest-main build, full-module pytest, and live HTTP/SSE integration were not run for this follow-up. Live text mode remains unverified.

title: test(vllm): allocate the self-benchmark disagg worker ports
body:
Source issue: [DYN-4252](https://linear.app/nvidia/issue/DYN-4252).

## Summary:

The disaggregated self-benchmark test left three worker listener ports at fixed values the shared test port allocator does not know about. When another process on the host holds one, the worker cannot bind, engine-core initialization fails, and the test reports that the server process exited while waiting for a health check. This change allocates all three from the shared ranges.

## Details:

In `tests/vllm_self_benchmark/test_self_benchmark_gpu.py`, `_DynamoBenchmarkWorker` already drew its system and forward-pass-metric ports from the allocator. Three listeners did not:

- the prefill worker's KV-events publisher, fixed at `20082`;
- the prefill worker's NIXL side channel, fixed at `5601`;
- the decode worker's NIXL side channel, never set, so it fell back to vLLM's host-wide default of `5600`.

Both disagg workers run with `--kv-transfer-config`, so both open a NIXL handshake listener. The side-channel port now comes from the `NIXL` range for every worker that opens one, and the prefill worker's KV-events endpoint from the `SERVE` range. Both new ports join the existing `allocated_ports` list, which the existing finalizer releases, so teardown is unchanged. No assertion changed.

This removes one identified cause of the reported startup failure. It does not establish that the test's remaining intermittent failures are gone.

## Where should the reviewer start?

`_DynamoBenchmarkWorker.__init__`, at the environment and command setup for the disagg pair.

## Validation:

With `5600`, `5601` and `20082` held by an unrelated listener, the test fails on `main` with `Address already in use` and passes on this branch; a control holding only `5600` reproduces the same bind failure in the decode worker. Ten clean repetitions and the untouched aggregated test also passed.

## Related Issues

**🔗 This PR is linked to an issue:**

- Closes [DYN-4252](https://linear.app/nvidia/issue/DYN-4252)

title: feat(profiler): runtime binding resolution
body:
## Summary
 
Implements item 3 of [tracking issue #13545](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/13545): "Bind the target runtime/backend version, compatible renderer, and matching performance data" — given one Candidate, resolves `runtime_image`, `num_gpus_per_node`, and `renderer`.
 
 
## What each piece resolves, and from where
 
- **`runtime_image`** — `{backend}-runtime:{backend_version}` on `nvcr.io/nvidia/ai-dynamo`, the exact convention used by every real DGD materialized throughout this work, formalized here rather than hand-supplied per call site.
- **`num_gpus_per_node`** — via `aiconfigurator.sdk.task_v2._lookup_num_gpus_per_node`. **See "Real, live verification" below — this one has an open dependency issue.**
- **`renderer`** — `"direct"` unless `(backend, strategy)` is a known gap (confirmed empirically: `TrtllmConfigModifier.set_config_tep_size`/`set_config_dep_size` raise `NotImplementedError` for the direct renderer), falling back to `"aic"` for exactly those combinations.
- **Performance-data matching** — via `aiconfigurator.sdk.common.check_support(model=, system=, backend=, version=, architecture=)`. Deliberately checks `result.agg_supported` vs. `result.disagg_supported` based on the candidate's own `deployment_mode`, not a blanket check — these are independent booleans in the real result shape, and checking the wrong one would silently accept a candidate that can't actually be rendered.
No matching performance data raises `RuntimeBindingError` — an ordinary, per-candidate outcome (skip this candidate, keep searching), not a terminal failure of the whole run, matching how `MaterializationError` is already handled one layer up.
 
## ⚠️ Open dependency issue: `_lookup_num_gpus_per_node` isn't in any released version yet,
exists on `main` branch  **not** exist in `0.11.0` — the latest version on the package index (`pip index versions aiconfigurator`).
- The raw hardware-catalog files it would read (`systems/*.yaml`, confirmed to contain the real `node.num_gpus_per_node` field) also aren't shipped anywhere in the installed package — so there's no client-side fallback available either.
 
**This is not a blocker for this PR**: `lookup_num_gpus_per_node` is an injectable dependency (`NumGPUsPerNodeLookup` protocol), so the real function can be wired in once released, with no changes to `resolve_runtime_binding` or any caller.
 

## Files
 
- `components/src/dynamo/profiler/sweeper/runtime_binding.py` (new)
- `components/src/dynamo/profiler/tests/unit/sweeper/test_runtime_binding.py` (new)

title: fix(tests): resolve AISimulate from NVIDIA index in wheel smoke tests
body:
Source issue: [DYN-4508](https://linear.app/nvidia/issue/DYN-4508).

## Summary

The wheel smoke tests now take `aisimulate` as a wheel from NVIDIA's package index, removing the step that made `test_core_install_clean_room[3.13]` fail intermittently.

## Details:

`ai-dynamo` requires `aisimulate==0.12.0` on Python 3.11-3.13, and the public index serves no wheel for that version — only a 20 kB placeholder sdist whose build backend downloads the real 83.6 MB `cp311-abi3` wheel at metadata time and asserts its SHA-256. One corrupted download made `pip install` exit 1 with `metadata-generation-failed`. pip's `--retries` and `--timeout` do not govern that transfer, which runs inside the build backend.

`pip_install` in `tests/wheels/smoke_install.py` adds `--find-links https://pypi.nvidia.com/aisimulate/` only when the wheelhouse has no AISimulate wheel, and passes `--only-binary aisimulate` to avoid the placeholder build backend. The dependency consistency guard checks the smoke helper's index URL against the expected NVIDIA URL and the Dockerfile's link source. `container/templates/wheel_builder.Dockerfile` already stages the wheel this way, but only for the planner and framework runtime targets, so the framework-agnostic `dynamo-runtime` image that runs these tests is not covered. The link source is scoped to one project page. The fallback requires `pypi.nvidia.com` to be reachable, as the placeholder already did; if it is not, the install fails with a plain resolution error naming `aisimulate`.

## Where should the reviewer start?

`pip_install` in `tests/wheels/smoke_install.py`, alongside lines 635-653 of `container/templates/wheel_builder.Dockerfile`.

## Validation

Prior validation at `3590f2a7b0faba45df0e3f1f9735ea4b0906ca76`: calling `pip_install` directly on Python 3.13 against an empty wheelhouse resolves the wheel with no metadata-preparation step; the same call without the added link source exits 1. The full node needs released `ai-dynamo` wheels, so only the `dynamo-runtime / test / parallel` job exercises it end to end — this shows the fragile path is no longer executed, not that a rare corrupted download has stopped occurring.

The consistency-guard update passes the repository-pinned isort, Black, Flake8, and Ruff checks. Runtime validation uses remote CI; no local tests or builds were run for this update.

## Related Issues

Closes https://linear.app/nvidia/issue/DYN-4508

title: feat(runtime): start every discovery watch with one resync snapshot
body:
Fixes #15066. Follow-up to #14769.

## Summary

Every `Discovery::list_and_watch` stream now starts with the state at establishment as one
`Added` event per matching instance and then exactly one `DiscoveryEvent::Resync` of the same
set, empty when nothing matches. A consumer that reopens a watch after losing one replaces its
state with that `Resync` and needs no `list()` call; an instance that left during the gap is
absent from the snapshot.

Design decision: the initial `Added` events stay, and the `Resync` follows them. Every existing
consumer either replaces its state on `Resync` with a set it already holds (no double-count, no
republish) or ignores `Resync`.

Per backend:

- **KV stores (etcd, file, memory):** `Bucket::watch` sends the existing entries as one
  `WatchEvent::Resync` instead of a `Put` burst, so the discovery layer's existing resync
  translation ends the startup burst with the snapshot. The discovery stream,
  `TypedPrefixWatcher`, and `KvCache` log the first resync at debug and a later one at warn. The
  NATS store is not a discovery backend and keeps its `Put` replay.
- **Kubernetes:** the daemon reports `Pending`/`Ready`/`Stopped`/`Failed` on a watch channel and
  sends `Ready` only after both reflectors completed their initial list and the result is in
  `list_state`. `list_and_watch` and `list` wait for `Ready` and fail when the daemon stopped or
  failed first, instead of returning an empty set the caller cannot tell from an empty cluster.
  The wait is unbounded while a reflector retries its initial list (unreachable API server, RBAC
  denial); the trait doc states this. `list_and_watch` stops waiting when the caller's
  cancellation token fires. `list()` waiting for readiness is a deliberate change to a second
  method, for consistency with the watch.
- **Mock:** one `Resync` after the `Added` burst.

Consumer audit (every `list_and_watch` caller in `lib/` and `lib/bindings/python`):

- Replace-on-`Resync`, unchanged set: `component/client.rs` (`EndpointDiscoverySource`),
  `llm/discovery/controller.rs` (revision-guarded), `llm/kv_dc_relay/discovery.rs`
  (`replace_all` reports no change), `llm/discovery/runtime_configs.rs` (no republish).
- Ignore `Resync`: `llm/discovery/{endpoint_card,kv_source_watch,watcher}.rs`,
  `llm/direct_zmq_fan_in.rs`, `llm/kv_router/indexer/recovery/{direct_zmq,state_agent}.rs`,
  `llm/kv_router/publisher/state_agent_host.rs`, `runtime/discovery/utils.rs`,
  `runtime/pipeline/network/egress/push_router.rs`,
  `runtime/transports/event_plane/dynamic_subscriber.rs`, `bindings/python/rust/llm/fpm.rs`.
- Re-list on every event: `llm/kv_router/publisher/attachment_owner.rs` and
  `llm/kv_dc_relay/membership_watch.rs` do one extra `list()` per new watch at startup. Benign.

Out of scope, for follow-up issues: `push_router.rs` watchers reconnect on stream end but keep
their dispatch and indexer state and ignore `Resync`, so the new snapshot does not yet remove an
instance that left during their gap; a Kubernetes watch opened before a post-`Ready` daemon
failure keeps serving and never errors (pre-existing, now observable through `DaemonState`).

## Validation

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo clippy -p dynamo-runtime --tests -- -D warnings` at every
  commit, `cargo clippy -p dynamo-llm --no-default-features --tests -- -D warnings`.
- `cargo test -p dynamo-runtime --lib`: 825 passed. `cargo test -p dynamo-llm
  --no-default-features --lib -- runtime_configs kv_dc_relay::discovery`: 23 passed.
- The shared startup contract (`discovery::startup_contract`) runs against the memory, file, and
  mock backends in two cases. An empty registry gives one empty `Resync`. A populated one gives
  its `Added` events and one `Resync` of the complete set, and a registration, a model taint
  update, and a removal made right after `list_and_watch` returns all follow that snapshot, which
  still holds the pre-change state.
- The Kubernetes stream is checked against a cluster-less client: the initial set, then one
  `Resync`, then later changes; a pending daemon holding the watch until `Ready` or
  cancellation; a stopped or failed daemon failing `list` and `list_and_watch`. The daemon test
  checks that `Ready` waits for both initial lists and follows the `list_state` write. The etcd
  store's initial `Resync` has a live-etcd test.
- Reconnect: a consumer replaces its state on the first `Resync` of a fresh stream.
  `a_resync_replaces_the_instances_of_a_discovery_source` covers replacement, and the contract
  tests prove each backend's snapshot content.
- Mutation check: dropping the startup `Resync` on memory, file, mock, and Kubernetes, letting
  readiness follow one initial list, and removing the cancellation race each turn a test red.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **New Features**
  - Discovery and storage watches now begin with a complete snapshot, including explicitly empty snapshots.
  - Resynchronization provides authoritative state for recovery after reconnects or missed updates.
  - Kubernetes discovery waits for readiness before returning data and reports failures or stoppages instead of exposing incomplete results.

- **Bug Fixes**
  - Prevented duplicate updates when startup events are followed by unchanged resynchronization snapshots.
  - Improved handling of removals and state changes during reconnects and synchronization.

title: perf(bindings): release gil during kv hashing
body:
## Overview: Release the Python GIL while the KV hashing binding performs pure Rust block-hash computation and converts the resulting hashes to `u64` values. This lets unrelated Python threads make progress during that native section without changing hash semantics. This PR is a contribution from [Fireworks AI](https://fireworks.ai). The change is generic to Dynamo and includes no customer-specific code, data, configuration, or operational details. ## Details: - Keep Python argument extraction and multimodal metadata conversion under the GIL. - Run `compute_block_hash_for_seq` inside `Python::allow_threads` using only Rust-owned or Rust-borrowed data. - Convert local block-hash wrappers to `Vec` before reacquiring the GIL. - Preserve `block_mm_infos`, `lora_name`, `cache_namespace`, and `is_eagle` behavior. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Python call] --> B[Extract arguments and MM metadata
GIL held] B --> C[Compute block hashes
GIL released] C --> D[Collect u64 results
GIL released] D --> E[Return Python result
GIL reacquired] ``` ## Related implementation precedent [Dynamo PR #12762](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/12762), authored by @nv-tusharma, established the same PyO3 pattern in this binding file: accept a `Python<'_>` token and wrap Rust work in `py.allow_threads` so another Python thread can remain responsive. The motivation and scope differ: - #12762 fixed a correctness issue where `KvRouter.__new__` could hold the GIL across an unbounded worker-registration wait, preventing Python timeouts and supervision from running. - This PR applies the established boundary to bounded CPU hashing. Python argument extraction still holds the GIL; only block hashing and conversion of Rust hash wrappers to `u64` values run without it. - Both changes cross the GIL boundary only with Rust-owned or Rust-borrowed values. PyO3's `allow_threads`/`Ungil` bounds enforce that Python-bound references are not used while the GIL is released. ## Where should the reviewer start? `lib/bindings/python/rust/llm/kv.rs`, specifically `compute_block_hash_for_seq_py`. ## Related Issues **🚫 This PR is NOT linked to an issue**: - [x] Confirmed — no related issue ## Summary - reduce the GIL-held portion of the Python KV hashing binding - preserve the existing API and hash outputs - add no new request-path allocation or Python call ## Validation - `cargo fmt --all -- --check` - `cargo test --manifest-path lib/bindings/python/Cargo.toml --lib` — 52 passed - `cargo clippy --manifest-path lib/bindings/python/Cargo.toml --lib -- -D warnings` - `git diff --check` ## Reviewer Ask This is a draft while concurrency evidence is refined. Please focus eventual review on the safety of the values captured by `allow_threads` and consistency with the pattern established in #12762. The hashing algorithm and Python argument-conversion API are unchanged and are not part of the review request. ## Perf Evidence **Evidence pending — draft, not ready for substantive review.** - This does not claim faster single-call hashing or higher aggregate throughput; it only shortens GIL ownership during existing pure Rust work. - CPU sanity: no new Python calls, hash operations, or allocations are added. Existing hash computation and result conversion move into `allow_threads`. - GPU sanity: this CPU-only binding change adds no GPU work, synchronization, kernel launches, or fences. Made with [Cursor](https://cursor.com) ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Performance** * Improved responsiveness during block-hash computation by allowing other Python threads to run concurrently. * **Compatibility** * Hash inputs, validation behavior, and returned values remain unchanged.

title: feat(epp): register shared router metrics without DRT
body:
## Summary

Expose the existing `dynamo_component_router_*` request metrics from standalone EPP without constructing a DRT. The EPP registers only the three families it can observe, reducing the work and payload of each `/metrics` scrape. The existing DRT/component constructor still registers the full set with unchanged names, labels, buckets, and observations.

The EPP records admitted selections and input tokens after `select_and_reserve`, and output tokens only when the backend reports `usage.completion_tokens` (including zero). It does not infer router TTFT, ITL, KV overlap, or completion counts from response byte chunks. Request-boundary metrics and phase timing remain in #15056.

## Details

- Add `RouterRequestMetrics::from_registry(registry, prefix, const_labels)` and a filtered `from_registry_subset` using the same metric definitions; cover schema compatibility and registry isolation.
- Register `requests_started_total`, `input_sequence_tokens`, and `output_sequence_tokens` with deployment-bound `model` and `inference_pool` labels on the EPP's existing private `/metrics` registry; test real gRPC observation paths and coexistence with `dynamo_epp_cached_tokens`.
- Document exactly which router families appear on the EPP endpoint. Families without an EPP observation source are absent rather than exporting misleading zero series.

The shared `dynamo_component_router_*` name follows the proposed reuse direction in #15058. The design discussion still has an open concern about whether an EPP-specific prefix would better distinguish observer semantics; this draft leaves that decision visible for review. Worker-state gauges, JSONL/config parity, and `picks_inflight` are outside this change.

title: feat(router): add do_not_queue admission control
body:
## Summary

Implement `do_not_queue` for #10573 against main at `f80421807`. An opted-in request now enters the normal policy queue and participates in class, deadline, priority, DRR, and worker eligibility decisions. After that admission turn drains, the router retracts the request only if it still needs to wait for worker capacity. Retraction restores global and class pending counters and disarms its lifecycle lease; the rejection reports the class load remaining after retraction. Ordinary requests continue to queue.

- Preserve `nvext.do_not_queue` and raw `RouterRequest::New.do_not_queue`, defaulting to `false`. Propagate the field through frontend, selection, standalone selection, and EPP. Advisory selection ignores it because advisory operations do not enter queue admission.
- Preserve structured raw `RouterResponse::DoNotQueue`. HTTP paths expose the distinct `router.do_not_queue` reason, `RateLimited`/429, and safe class and pending load details. Existing queue-limit, deadline, capacity, and no-worker outcomes retain their own behavior.
- Update the existing nvext documentation and all affected custom-policy example, builtin scorer, and benchmark constructors.

This option governs only the router pending queue. It does not control backend engine queues or guarantee zero end-to-end waiting. Existing high-level positional routing APIs retain their default behavior; the PR does not extend the C API.

## Validation

- macOS: `cargo test -p dynamo-kv-router --no-default-features --features standalone-selection do_not_queue --lib` (14 passed), plus all 51 scheduler queue tests without default features.
- macOS: targeted `dynamo-llm --no-default-features` tests cover semantic error mapping, raw router idle/busy behavior, and real unary and streaming HTTP 429 responses. Targeted `dynamo-ext-proc` tests cover integrated and standalone EPP mappings. The HTTP and raw router integration tests used a localhost-capable test environment.
- `cargo check` passed for `dynamo-ext-proc`, `dynamo-custom-policy-builtin`, and the two affected custom-policy examples. `cargo fmt --all -- --check` and `git diff --check` passed. Docs lint passed with 0 errors and 8 existing warnings.
